ORDIFINRY BRANCH. —The number of polices issued during the )ear was '19,942, assuring the sum of £7,529.031, and producing a new annual premium income of £424,145. The premiums received during the year were £1.290.971, being an increase of £167,653, over the year 1905. The claims of the year amounted to £1 947 444. The number of deaths was 7,656. and 8,686 endOwment assurances matured. The number of policies in force at the end of the year was 807,218. INDUSTRIAL BRANCH.—The premiums received during the year were £6,499,028, being an increase of £259,978. The claims of the year amounted to £2,276,863. The number of deaths was 260,941, and 3.342 endowment assurances matured. The number of free pnlices granted during the year to those policy-holders of five years' standing and upwards who desired to discontinue their payments, was 120,198, tbe number in force being 1 194.02. 't he number of free polices which became claims during the year was 28.034. The total number of polices In force at the end of the year was 16.764,654 ; their average duration exceeds eleven years. The assets of the company. in both branches, as shown in the balance sheet, are £63,887,038, being an increase of 24,422 632 over those of 1905. The increase granted early in the year under the prineipal Industrial Branch tables. to provide for which £750,000 was transferred from reserve, affected nearly thirteen million policies, ten millions of which received an immediate Increase in the sum assured. The Directors are glad to say that the alteration hae been highly appreciated, and has resulted in a large acceision of new susinees. As the shareholders ake aware. the Directors have on menV °mations granted extended benefits to Industrial Branch policyholders. 'I he total cost of these benefits already exceeds £4,000,000. It is the intention of the Di,e store to continue this policy, and if postible to establlsh it upon a more definite basis. light, bright shades of blue in the milliner's windows and showrooms, but whether these particular hues are the wisest choice for early spring, may be quelled. At this season of the year, the keen winds play more or less havoc with our complexions, when the present modish blues do not always prove becoming. Bright ; cornflower blue is one shade we should all do well to ' avoid. It emphasises sallowness to quite an extra-' ordinary degree while a pale face looks livid beneath it. I Indeed it kills the most perfect complexions,even when ; at their very best. Periwinkle blues too, are dangerous in this respect and even the least vain among us may I be pardoned for carefully studying the effect of head- gear built up of these particular shades before investing in a purchase. Coins as Weights.—ln an emergency, coins will be I found to make good substitutes for weights. For I example three pennies weigh one ounce, while a two shilling piece and a sixpence together, equal half-an- ounce. A quarter of an ounce may be arrived at by means of a threepenny bit, and a halfpenny together. MADGE. I

After one or two years. find- ing that summer is perpetual and flowers forever abundant, she will live from day to day content to gather the honey and pollen indispensable for the day's consumption; and, her recent sod thoughtful observation triumphing over here- ditary experience, she will, cease to make provi- sion for her winter. Btielmer mentions an ana- logous fact, which- also Proves the bees' adapta- tion to circumstances, not slow, secular, uncon- scious and fatal, but immediate and intelligent: in Barbados, the bees • whose hives are in the midst of the refineries. where they find sugar in plenty during the whole year. will entirely abr,. don their visits to the flowers.

POLICE SUPERINTENDENT CHALLENGED.
raising powder

At Runcorn Police Court on Monday, Ellen Dyer, licensee of the Waterloo Hotel, was summoned for per- mitting drunkenness. On the 15th of last month Sergeant Allenby, accompanied by Constable Wynne, went into the bar parlour of the hotel. There were four men present, including a man named Parry. The latter said, "What's up?" and the sergeant replied," I heard loud talking." He at once saw that Parry was drunk. The Sergeant pointed out his condition,and the defendant said, " Yes, you had better go home; you are tipsy." The defence was that Parry was not drunk, and was talking rationally about music. At the police station to show he was sober Parry offered to run or sing the superintendent for a sovereign. The bench said there would not be a conviction,but defendant must pay the costs. Parry was fined 105. and costs.

div.p: WOMAN'S REALM.
DRESS-FASHION-1101N1E.
THE COUNTESS "CABBY."

Among the women who have qualified as cab- drivers in Paris is one who is a Countess in her own right. Born Comtesse de la, Gueriniere, Madame Lutgen before her marriage was de- voted to sport of every kind, and from her earliest girlhood was an excellent whip. Her hus- band's recent loss of his position as leading tenor in a Paris church has impoverished the house- hold, and the Countess has pluckily determined to turn her driving powers to account, and so help to provide for her three little children. Some of the leading members of the old French aristo- cracy, amongst whom is the Duchesse d'Uzes, have publicly applauded the young Countess for the step she has taken, and her cab is not likely to lack patronage.

div.head: HATS AND TRIMMINGS.
div.p: HATS AND TRIMMINGS.

A tendency is once again shown where small hats are concerned to relegate the most import- ant part of the trimming to the back of the hat instead of the front or side. This is specially noticeable .in the case of the new headgear with high dome-shaped crown. , trimmed with wide soft ribbon in two shades, which is swathed round the crown and arranged in mammoth loops and bows at the back, with the addition of a quantity of flowers or plumes. Such a hat is by no means generally becoming, but it is. nevertheless, rapidly gaining in popularity, and for morning wear will undoubtedly be high in favour. _ _

div.head: LADY CLIFTON ROBINSON.
div.p: LADY CLIFTON ROBINSON.

Among the most. notable presentations ,at the first Court, says the Sketch. was that of Lady Clifton Robinson, the beautiful Irish wife of tins great engineer who has earned in two hemi- spheres the nickname of "the Tramway King." Lady Clifton Robinson possesses, in the matter of dress, all the genius of her nation, and of the many "bullion" frocks worn at the February Courts, her exquisite costume stood out. as an admirable example of 'grace and originality. Thu gown, of white. net, was richly embroidered in silver, each panel being edged and completed with a fairy-like diamond web, from which fell a—diamant6 fringe terminating in Femtned trel- lis-work. The white tulle bodice, lightly draped with diamond-studded. lace. was -embroidered with a spray of silver roses; and, most effective touch of all, the cloth-of-silver .train was lined ,With green, and exquisitely embroidered by hand.

The CHAIRMAN said that personally he did not see what arrangements could be come to although there seemed to be a better feeling. The Labour Representa- tion Committee were very sore about the action of the Council in trying to bring about the unification of the trades in the town. Whether they succeeded or not in their endeavour he did not think anything could be done by prolonging the life of the Labour Representa- tion Committee, Mr. GRBALEY : It is not intended to prolong the life of the Labour Representative Committee. Councillor STOTT seconded. The Council need have no fear that the Labour Representative Committee would be able to convince the Council that they had done wrong. r. GaRkLEY : What is the use of discussing it? We have decided to leave the Labour Representative Committee.

Mr. PODNIORE said he believed the conference might lead to the unificttion of the labour forces of the town. div.head: UNEMPLOYED QU ESTION.
div.p: UNEMPLOYED QU ESTION.

The Joiners' representative moved that a resolution be sent to Nlr. A. H. Crostleld kf.P. expressing regret that there was no mention in the King's speech of the unemployed question and asking the Government at an early date to deal with " this serious and . menacing evil."
The resolution was unanimously approver'. PRESENTATION TO COUNCMLOR STOTT.

Tht cancltiding business of the meeting was of a pleasant character consisting of the presentation of a clock and bronzes, suitably inscribed, to Councillor Stott in recognition of his valuable services as secretary of the Council.

Mr. Mooluta.% as secretary of the Presentation Committee, explained that the proposal had been carried through with the greatest enthusiasm. Mr. PODMORE, who said he was probably the oldest member of the Council, paid a high tribute to the ser- vices rendered by Councillor Stott. They had in Councillor Stott a man who had devoted his life to the uplifting of his fellow men and who had spared neither time nor effort in the desire to attain that end. The Trades Council entered upon a new era when Councillor Stott became the secretary and he had raised it to a level which it never before attained in Warrington. In his work he had displayed great energy and ability, and what was even more, had shown initiative. He looked upon the present as a small token of the regard which they had for Councillor Stott's work not only on behalf ' of the Trades Council but on behalf of labour gener- ally, and they hoped that Councillor Scott would long be spared to carry on the splendid work and that others would he induced to follow his example. Messrs. Plinston, Haley, Massey, and Pook joined in the general expression of good wishes. The CHAMAI AN in making the presentation said Coun- cillor Stott's onlyfault was that he had not sulicient regard for self and constantly endangered his health by undertaking sa much work on behalf of labour. Councillor STOTT feelingly returned thanks. His ambition had always been to persuade every trade union branch in Warrington to become affiliated with the Council, and he hoped they would not rest satisfied until they had achieved that object. (Hear, hear.) He thanked them for the present to himself and his wife. He could assure them that had it not been for the assist- ance which his wife had given to him, he would not have been able to accomplish the work which he had undertaken. In regard to the future he was confident that if they remained in the old rut they would never as a trades council be that force which they ()tight to be in Warrington. (Applause).

The Whiteeross Ward Contest.

Mr. Plumb presided over a large attendance at the Monthly meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council held at the Bold-street schools on Tuesday. The first question under discussion was the Guardians •election. Mr. James Heywood, the nominee of the Socialist party in the Whitecross Ward, wrote as a member of the assurance agent's Society asking the Council to endorse his candidature. Mr. GREA.LEY moved that the request be not eater- tamed. If they opposed Councillor Evans they were oPPosing a friend. There were plenty of enemies of labour whom Mr. Heywood could fight without select- ,lllg a friend. He thought Mr. Eleywood should try his luck with those who were the enemies of labour. , ,Mr. HALEY : Mr. Heywood is a Trade Unionist and Ins candidature is endorsed by his Society. Mr. GREAEEY rose to a point of order and during the brief discussion which followed it transpired that Alt* Heywood had not theofficialsnpport of his Society. Mr. HaLEv: Mr. Heywood was the first in the field. HICKINBOTTOM :. No. He was not. M.HAYLEY : 1 understand that he was and there- h°te it is not Mr. Heywood who is opposing Mr. Evans Mr. Evans who is opposing a progressive trade aionist and socialist. .Mr HICKNBOTTOM : I know that is not so. Coun- cil' • • or Evans was brought forward first and then to his Prise Mr. Heywood was nominated by the Labour .11.1Y1r. POOK said that as a Labour man and a trade utunnist they were in duty bound to support Mr. ikeYwood and not bolster up an employer of labour. uey were continually fighting labour and it was the Mt thing they should be asked to do to support a Illaster and ask a trade unionist to stand down. if Mr. GREALEY : We are bound to have employers and pWe have a good one why should we oppose him. Mr. tlYans always has been a good employer of labour. Mr. iteYwood could find plenty of enemies if he looked round ge different wards instead of fighting the best man nut. On a vote being taken it was decided by 15 to 4 ,to 'indorse the candidature of Mr. Heywood.

This is ?specially detrimental as carpentering is gradually uelng superseded by steel and other materials and the Market for this tr ide is already over-stocked." • The JOINERS' DELEGATE moved that a resolution of Protest be sent to the Education Committee. They di ?lot think it was right that lads should be taught joiner- in the Beamont or any elementary school. They !lid not object to the teaching of the trade in the Fechnical School for, as a rule,students there were serv- Irig an apprenticeship. Mr. GREALEY heartily supported the motion. Ho would bject most strongly if they proposed to teach baking in the elementary schools. „ Mr. MAssEv also supported the motion. He thought 'lie teaching of the trade was a great injustice to those lads who were serving an apprenticeship. , The CHAIRMAN asked how far they were prepared to o go. It was just as reasonable for clerks to protest Itgainst lads recei,7ing an education which would befit them to become clerks. If they were going to prohibit 147137 subject they would do an injustice to the children. NIL MASSEY thought there WAS a great difference ,11511. tween teaching a boy, to become a clerk and teaching ,1112 to be a joiner. These boys acquired a certain c,echnical knowledge by the time they reach the age of '4 and undersold in the labour market. If it was pro- 15°Bed to teach boys practical engineering he would tsove in the matter himself. It was decided to postpone the question pending the result of enquiries from the Beamont School managers.

div.head: MILITARY TRAINING.
div.p: MILITARY TRAINING.
IS OUR ;`,IOUNIRY SAFE?
Criticism of the Labour Party.

A public !noting promoted by the Warrington branch of the National Service League was held in the Co- operative Hall, Sankey-street.on Tuesday evening when Mr. Leo Maxse, editor of the "National Review," spoke on" Our country, is it safe ?" Tn the absence of : Mr. W. P. Rylands, fr. H. Roberts presided over a good attendance. Prior to the meting musical items were contributed by a male glee party and Arr. Ford, (pianist.) In the course of a letter NTr. RVLINDS said : "Meng sang, in corpore sano " should he our watchword, tlnd in my opinion it is only by an intelligent and eompulsory system of physical training that rve can get the full benefit from the millions of money now spent upon education.

The CRAIRM AN seid public opinion lwel grown most 'irapicily in favour of the League durine the last few years and more nerticniarly, bethought, during the past few weeks. There were only two possible policies before them. They were all convinced that the volun- tary systemhad failed absolutely. Whether it could be patched no he Mr. Haldane's proposals so as to make it do a little longer or nrt remained to be seen ; but whether that should he so or net, what people were getting convinced about was that a man had no right to devolve any part of his duty noon his fellow. As a fiiberal he had no hesitation in miring it was perfectly consistent wish tree Liberalism that men should do for themselves what the cone try reqiiired—(applause)—and be thought it wee the truest Conservatism that demanded the same condition of things. (Applause.) Mr. LEO ITAXSE in the course of a most interesting address emphasised the imnortance of interesting the working classes in the question.nninting out that as the principal votine rower they had become responsible for the safety of the Stete.No Cabinet 'meld exsist any length of time without the support and annroval of the masses and he thought he might say that, though he was a Unionist, when they lately saw a Government endeavour- ing to outstay its welcome,it was very heavily punished for it. The democracy was now in possession of Great Britain and if any disaster happened to England it would lie at the door of the democracy and it was 'against the democracy that posterity would enter its verdict. Unfortunately the Labour leaders who claimed to represent the working classes had, he ventured to say, not risen to the height of their responsi- bility upon this and kindred questions. The only interest which they had taken so far in the question of national defence was as to the amount of wages which were paid in the dockyards and arsenals and other Government establishments—which was no doubt a very important matter from the working class point of view, but it was not the most important matter for there was something to be considered before they came to that. Mr. Kier Hardie, the leader of the Labour party in the House of Commons, was universally regarded as a transparently honest man who had no axe of his own to grind and who was much lass self-seeking than a great many other politicians. He had been frank enough to tell them that heaimed at making the class to r;hich he belonged supreme in the State. But unfor- tunately Mr. Kier Hardie absolutely declined to take any steps to give security to the State—in fact he had thrown his influence on the side of the seatimentalists who cultivated all those dangerous delusions with regard to brotherly love entertained by foreigners toWards this country and had made a series of speeches which really reminded one of nothing except of the early Victorian days when poets used to sing of " The Parlia- ment of man, the federation of the world." It was 'a very serious question for the working classes,-because if they followed Mr. Kier Hardie's view on this and other questions they might conceivably become supreme in the State but it. would be an unarmed State, and how long did they think an unarmed nation would be able in this wicked world in which we lived, to preserve its independence among the armed nations? When we allowed our armaments to fall below a certain level,we would instantly become the prey of some stronger power, and the power which at the present day kept the sharpest eye upon us was Germany. In Germany there was very bitter hostility between the German Kier Hardies and the Government and he would like to ask Mr. Kier Hardie as to what sort of a show lie thought he would have if by any mischance things went wrong with us and he found himself a subject of the mailed fist; because as far as he (Mr. Merse) could make cut. Mr. Kier Hardie's policy upon all these questions of national defence was to leave this country absolutely at the mercy of Germany. Continuing Mr. Maxse said he had discusssed the question with many foreigners who contended that if owing to our apathy and indifference on the question of national defence we should not pre- serve our influence as the great liberal power,the world and especiglly Europe would pass to the domination of the reactionaries. A Socialist leader from abroad had expressed surprise at the attitude of the Labour party in England which he described as undemocratic, and un-social on this question. The voluntary system. said Mr. Mane, divorced the nation from the army and threw the burden of defending the country on the few. It created a military caste and developed all the worst evils of militarism. They ought to recognize the importance of keeping the question absolutely clear of party prejudice. (Applause.) The attitude of the Labour party was rather disappointing to him and to others, because they had hoped that as the Labour men were new as a party to Politics and were not trammelled by the traditions which paralysed so many hack politicians, they would introduce a touch of reality on this question as well as on many others. Unfortunately he had not noticed any Labour member had vet spoken the word in season, but he was clad to have been able to find a word in season in the Socialist paper "The Clarion" which in an editorial contended that the burden of defence should be shared by all good citizens and that military training would benefit the physique of the people. The pro- gramme of the National Service League was not con- scription or anything remotely resembling it, but was system of absolutely democratic equality which would cast equal duties on all citizens. lie believed it NVIIS generally agreed that if the young men of this country ' went through a period of six months' military training, it would be enough for all national purposes and would be an incalculable advantage to them. He believed England was in a position of considerable danger at the present time. She seemed to be con- fronted by the relentless determination of the most powerful of Continental countries to challenge ourposi- tion on this planet. The Germans were a very formidable people of some sixty rnillions,and the German Govern- ment seemed to he gradually convincing the German people that England was the obstruction which must be swept aside before Germany could hope to obtain that place in the world which she regarded as the one to which she was entitlet Our Navy was our sole enarantee of our existence and of our bread and better. Germany was spending no less than £300,000,000 in building a navy. That was £50,000,000 more than we spent on the South African war. It was clearly not a defensive weapon, because the German defence rested on the German Army. The ships already constructed were of very small coal-carrying capacity and were not. he felt convinced, to defend Germany against the United States or Janne. They were intended to operate not far away, and that mighty squadron remained glued to the North Sea save when they were allowed by as to cruise in home waters, with vehicle the German naval °ricers were anxions to familiarize themselves, as they regarded that as the chosen battle ground of the future. He did not think we could afford to go on blinking the fact that the German navy was being built for one pur- pose alone—to challenge the sea power of England. There was no concealment, as it had actually been set out in the preamble of the Naval Bill of 1900 that Great Britain was the objective. it was absolutely insane of us to continue to ignore the fact that the German Navy ,V 51.3 intended to deal a blow at the heart of the British Emnire. Mr. iklnicse quoted from speeches of German officers and others which he believed pointed to this fact and revealed a very serious position. Unfortunately this country was full of self co mnlacentroptimiste who spent their time in explaining away every disagreeable fact, and the most dis- greeable fact from our point of view at the present time was the flotation of a great German fleet on an ocean of Anglophobia. We were not only doing nothing but less than nothing. We seemed to be knocking the few fragments of the army that were left to bits, and the present Government—and he did not say this because it was a Liberal Government as all governments were untrustworthy on the question of national defence—was tampering with the British Navy because they had forgotten that epigram of Lord Charles Beresford that battleships were cheaper titan battles. The whole world looked on and wondered. Our party statesmen seemed to think they disposed of the whole question by declaring that invasion was not within the eeeion of practical politics, and in the next breath they told them they intended to create a territorial army. The only way we could make invasion impracticable was by pre- paring for it. by arming the people. Put our national defence on to a national basis by instructing the whole of our citizens in the elementary eq. of self-defence end the navy would then acquire strategic freedom to carry out its proper function—to seek out and destroy the enemy's fleet. (Applause.) If we were apathetic or indifferent as to the futnre of our country, and careless Ise to whether we handed on that great heritage rh9h had been handed down to us. then there was nothing In this wide world which could prevent us suffering the fate which we should certainly deserve, and have the epitaph written on the tombstone of our country: "Here lies the mighty but eel f-eomnlaeent nation who tempted Providence once ton often." (Applause.) Mr. S. R. ARMITAGE proposed a vote of thanks to qr. Mn xse for his admirable address. He thought they could not do too mileh to push forward the prinsiples of the E.eague. Before that night, he h.d no intention of joining the Leagne, but in future, he should do all he could to persuade the working classes in Warrinoton to join it. In the old days, when they were at school, most of them had a " sergeant " in the playground. That was the only military diecinline he had had to carry him through life. (Laughter.) The time had come when each one of them, whether workman or master, should push forward that great enestion, and bring into their ranks men of every class. They bad no right to rely upon their neighbours. Each,

div.head: STOCKT3N HEATH AFFAIRS.
div.p: STOCKT3N HEATH AFFAIRS.
Parochial Committee and New Byelaws.

The monthly meeting of the Parochial Committee was held at the Hall Cafe, Victoria Square on Tuesday night. Mr. G. Pilling presided and there were also present Messrs. J. H. Clarke, F. Pearson. J. Hallows, J. Whitley, H. J. Westbrook, F. Warburton, J. Swinton (surveyor) and G. F. Ashton (clerk).

div.head: CLERK'S REMU. NERATIOII.
div.p: CLERK'S REMU. NERATIOII.
On the motion of Mr. Pearson, seconded by Mr. Hallows, the sam of £25 was allowed to the Clerk for his services during the past year.
THE NEW BYELAWS. TRIBUTE TO THE WORK OF THE CLERK AND SURVEYOR.

Mr. Clarke said they ought to recognise in some way the great increase in the work of the Clerk during the past year. It was well known to them that the Com- mittee had been revising the model byelaws submitted by the Local Government Board. They had been very carefully revised, and had been made more switable for a district like Stockton Heath, which was fast growing out of the sphere of a rural district to one of an urban district. The bvelaws which had been drawn up were applicable generally to rural districts. They had had the assistance of their Clerk at every one of the meet- ings, and he had come especially to Stockton Heath on many occasions during the past twelve months. He referred to the amount of time the Clerk had given to the work and the ability he had displayed in helping and guiding them in the framing of those bye-laws. What they had done would be of benefit to other parts of the Union. The amount that he was going to propose to be given to Mr. Ashton would not amply repay him for the work he had done, and he thought other parts of the union might be fairly called upon to contribute in some way. He proposed that a special donation of £5 be given to Mr. Ashton as an acknowledgement of his services and out of pocket expenses. In reply to Mr. Hallows, the Chairman said it was for exceptional work. Mr. H. J. Westbrook seconded, and said he apprecia- ted and endorsed alt that Nfr. Clarke had said. They all felt, without flattering the Clerk, that for courtesy, kindness, and urbanity, it would be a difficult thing to find his equal. Thet sum proposed was only a modest recognition of the work he had done, and other parts of the Union would benefit. He hoped it would be pointed out to other districts, and that they would make him some similar contribution. - - _

Mr. Ashton said he fully appreciated what Mr. Clarke and Mr. Westbrook had said. If the work he had done had been work that he could fairly consider was speci- ally chargeable to Stockton Heath he would have accepted the sum with very mat pleasure, bat he honestly felt that as far as bye-laws were concerned it was not work that should be charged specially against that parish. Peeling that,he thought it wouldbe wrong to let the resolution go to the committee without stating his own views on the point. If any remunera- tion was granted it should not be a special charge. If any building was done in the parish, it did not help that parish only but also other disiriots. He would certainly prefer that the resolution should be entirely withdrawn. because he felt that Stockton Heath should not be put to that expense alone, lie fully appreciated the kind remarks which had been made. Mr. Clarke said that after what had been said by Mr. Ashton, perhaps the suggestion he had made was the one to adopt. The District Council should deal with the matter as a whole, and if they (the Parochial Com- mittee) found the Clerk was not treated fairly it was in their hands te make a recommendation. There could be no harm in an opinion going from that meeting that Mr. Ashton's services should be acknowledged by the District Council. (Hear, hear). Mr. Swinton had also assisted them, and his services should also be recog- nised. He therefore coupled the suggestion with the resolution. _ _

Mr. H. J. Westbrook seconded, and the suggestion was agreed to. The Chairman said the original resolution was with- drawn. He rather liked the idea Mr. Clarke mentioned in the first place, but on taking a broad view Mr. Ash- ton was right. What had been done was for the benefit of the whole Union, and other districts should con- tribute.
Mr. Westbrook: Whatever the other districts decide we shall do our part. THE SURVEYOR'S REMUNICTt.i.TION.

Mr. Westbrook proposed and Mr. Pearson seconded that Mr. Swinton be allowed the sum of £lO for his services during the year. Mi. Whitley said that not only in the matter of bye- laws but in other matters, Mr. A.shton and Mr. Swinton were always ready to do anything to forward the interests of the parish. ([Tear, hear.) The motion was carried.

div.head: MORE LIGHTING_COMPLAINTS.
div.p: MORE LIGHTING_COMPLAINTS.

Mr. Pearson said that Mr. Bouchier was unable to be present at the meeting and he asked him to bring before the committee the fact that the bottom end of Walton. road was badly lighted. An arrangement was made with the Lower Walton Parish Council to light that Dart of Walton-road in exchange for the Stockton Heath Committee lighting Lawrenson's-brow. After a short discussion it was decided that the attention of the Walton Parish Council be called to the matter.

Mr. Hallows said he had received complaints of lamps not having been lighted in Stockton Heath. Mr. Clarke said he understood that the lamps should be lighted at sunset. but in Grappenhall-road they were seldom lighted within an hour after sunset. That night they were being lighted about 7.15. It was certainly very unsatisfactory. it was decided that the Clark write to the Gas Com- mittee on the matter.

div.head: PAVING OF STREETS AND PASSAGES.
div.p: THE PAVING OF STREETS AND PASSAGES.

The Chairman stated that on Saturday afternoon several members of the Committee met essrs. Garnett and Wright with respect to the paving of streets and back passages in the parish. The Committee gave them their opinion. and he moved Ihat the Clerk write to Niessrs. Garnett and Wright to push on with the work. Hr. Hallows said the feeling of the parish was that the work should be done as soon as possible. There was a considerable amount of grumbling going on.. The Clerk promised to write, and aided that Messrs. Garnett and Wright had had the specification since last December.

div.head: _THE PARISH COUNCIL RUCTIONS.
div.p: _THE PARISH COUNCIL RUCTIONS.

The Chairman said he was very pleased to find that many of the old faces would be seen at their future meetings. With regard to the forthcoming District Council Election he hoped the best men would get in.

div.head: STILL WELL AFTER 6 YEARS!
div.p: STILL WELL AFTER 6 YEARS!

div.head: CHIEF CONSTARTS TRAGIC END.
div.p: CHIEF CONSTARTS TRAGIC END.
SUICIDE IN It GAIT) MEL

The Painful sho::%-. which was eanse.l in -Warrington last Saturday by the neTs that Mr. Luke Tabot, the Chief Constable, had died sullenly at Ciiro, was . intensfied wh.n it bee,ame knova th it Mr. Talblt had taken away his nun life by s otin hinsalF in his hotel. Few public nrti'q iis were more highly esteemed for the canscientiousness and tact with which they dis- charged their dnties, than the late respected head of our Police Force, and his tragic end has occasioned genuine regret amoagst all classe: of the community. In particular the me.mbers of the Police Force sincerely deplore the loss of one who, took the keenest interest in their well-being and during the week they have been wearing crape bands, as a mark of r,spect. The deepest sympathy is felt with Mrs. Talbot in her bereavement.

The first briPf o-rtirydar. of 6. Chi 4 InsfiVA's death were conveyed in a cablezram to the Tomn Clerk which Carrie to hand on Saturday : "Talbot found dead in b3d with revolver, Nionday miming (week). Shot through heart. Buried on Tuesday at the British Cemetery. No doubt suicide, but verdict of jury not before Monday. At first thought AmericAn. His effects now in my custody. Will write. British Consul." k

_ The Cairo correspondent of the "Daily Telegriph " cabled as follows to Tuesday's issue of that journal: "An inquest was held yesterday (NfondaY) afternoon at the British Consular Court, on the body of Luke Talbot, late Chief (instable of Warrington, Lanca- shire. The deceased man was found dead in his rlom at a fashionable hotel in Cairo, with a revolver by his side containing two cartridges, one of which had been fired. Medical evidence showed that the bullet from the discharged cartridge had penetrated the heart, causing instantaneous death. A note written in pencil was discovered amongst the effects of the dead man, indicating that he was in a desperate condition, owing to what he alleged to be persecution. The jury returned a verdict of " Suicide whilst temnorarilv insane." LETTER FROM MR. TALBOT TO VIE TOWN CLERK.

The following is a copy of a charactgristio letter received by the Town Clerk from the late Nfr.Talbot : Eden Palace Hotel, Cairo (Egypt). Cair-o. vebruary 24th, 1907. Dear Friend,-1 am just dropping you a ling to lot you know that I am alive in the land of the Pharaohs— and things.

We had thirteen days' passage by sea to Port Said, stormy and cold all the way. I landed on Weinevlay (the 20th). This is Sunday, but no Sabbath in this wild whirl-a-gig of a Pentecostal City. Men, women, and children of every race under the sun are raising all kinds of Hades in the streets. squares and gardens. It is the Greek carnival. I have been up to see the Pyramids and the SohinK. These monu- ments of age and mystery are sufficiently weird in themselves, but to see Bedouins on camels and dromedaries just in from the desert jostling the electric tram (terminus—the Great Pyramid !) and luxurious motor landaus is the last word of topsv- turviness. Donkeys, camels, elephants all laden with tourists or dusky heathen, fight for room with smart four-in-hands tooled by unmistakable British officers. It is the most bewildering scene on earth (perhaps), with the grim desert for a background. The sun from 10 ft.m. to abouts p.m. is a scorcher. Then comes the brief twilight and with sunset a chill wind from the Sahara. Then one needs a wrap. lam still feeling the fatigue of the journey, though I do not sleep very well in suite of being tired. I wish I were back at work. T shall count the days until I fly my flag in dear old Warrington once again. Please drop me a line in reply. It is devilishly lonely in this huge gay crowd.—Yours most sincerely,
LUKE TALBOT.
J. L. Whittle, Esq. "COULD NOT SLEEP OR EAT."

On Thnrslay morning the Town Clerk received th following letter from Mr. F. S. Firmstone. of the New Khedive' Hotel, Cairo :—" Dear Sir.—Mr. Talbot, of Palmyra-square, died at the Eden Palace Hotel on Monday, the 4th inst.. in the early morning. He was in a very poor state of health, being unable to sleep or eat for several days prior to his decease. k letter addressed to him by his wife was never releivei by him, as it only arrivel on Tuesday morning—the day following his death. I am not sure whether the sad news has been oabled to her, but I feel confident that you will break the same to her friends, so that they may console her in her sad bereavement." A TOUCHING POEM.

Literature was Mr. Talbot's dearest hobby and one in which he displayed marked ability. Peculiar interest attaches to the following touching verses which he wrote on the occasion of the sudden death in the Isle of Man of the Police Court Missionary (Mr. Henry Taylor) :

IN NIEWORI AM. Peace!—it i well with him—ves. passing well, Called hence in haste as God's beloved guest, To sit at noonday in the Firma of Bast, While we toil even to the vesper bell. Swift came the bidding—for the Master knew How fit and ready for their Lord's decree Stand evermore such servitors as he From dawn-day to the rising of the dew. Our brothers bruised beneath ths penal rod. Healed of his hand. shall keen his memory green— Sole record of a life that toiled unseen— Save what is written in the Scrolls of GA. Priest 'of the poor, himself as poor as they, Pleader for Peace. and advocate of love, His was the wealth that wisdora hoards above— And he has come into his own to-day. Upon his lips no ItertflAnlie lore Only the wondrous Word's anglified gold, In simple speech as His who spoke of old To shipmen of the Galilean shore. Soldier of Christ—the record needs no gloss, Called from the lighting-line by swift command. T o be requited by the King's right hand, "'or valour" with the glory of the Cross. REFERENCES AT THE POLICE COURT.

Feeling references to the death of the Chief Constable were made at the Barough Police Court on Monday. The MAYOR (Alderman Smethurst) said he was expressing his own feelings, and the feeling of his brother magistrates and the public of Warrington when he said how deenlv they felt for the beloved wife of Kr. Talbot. Their Chief Constable was a man of many parts, and the Part he chose in the profession of the constabulary had evidently been the right choice, as, they all knew by .reading his career in the Press on Saturday last. He left them a short time ago, expect- ing to return with good health, so that he might follow his public duties. Unfortunately he was dead. He (the Mayor) had lost a friend, and he knew that a great many others in the town had also lost a friend. He was sure he was expressing the ?-eelings of the staff—from superintendent Monaghan and the inspectors down to the constables—when ha said they too had lost a good friend. Mr. Talbot might have been a strict master, but he had brought the force up to a position equal to any force in Lancashire. He (the Mayor) heal had the pleasure of meeting the Government Inspector several ti nes at the Police Station,and the Inspector had always expressed great satisfaction as to the way the members of the force did their duty, and as to their smart appearance. He felt certain that the impression which Mr. Talbot had left upon his men would not be lost, but that they would go on and prosper and obtain their right positions, as their late Chief had done. Mr. Talbot had done all he could for the town. They all knew the benefits that the Infirmary had received from the Police Athletic Sports which, he believed, were promoted by the Chief Constable and his staff. Mr. Talbot also showed Christian feelings towards many prisoners, and frequently asked the mercy of the court for them. Two days before he departed he (the Mayor) was in conversation with him, and referred to several matters. As showing Mr. Talbot's feelings, he promised on his return to do all he could to secure the liberty of the man Bate, who had been in 'prison ten years. He parted with good in his mind, and good in his heart. He (the Mayor) was sure they would 'all express their deep regret with the widow in her sad loss. Mr. W. ROBERTS said that in Mr. Talbot they had a man who was proud of the force and everyone under him, and a man who, he believed, conscientiously and faithfully endeavoured to discharged his duties. It had 13een painfullv evident to most of them that for a long time Mr. Talhothad been physically unfit for his duties but he struggled on manfully, with great physical weak- ness. They had all felt many times that he had been at his post when he was quite unfit to be there. Their hearts went out with tender sympathy to Mrs. Talbot, and they hoped and prayed that strength might be given to her to bear that great blow. The MAGISTRATES' CLERK (fr. G. F. F. White) briefly endorsed these remarks. The Deputy Town Clerk (Mr. HALLOWAY) said on behalf of Vie officials of the Corporation he would like to associate himself with every word so sympathetic- ally said. They not only knew that the town had lost an official whose work would always remain as a monu- ment to him, but they felt, each and everyone of them, that they oad lost a very sincere friend. Mr. BROWNE said it would ill befit the occasion if he did not say a few words on behalf of himself and fellow local solicitors practising in that Court. " Time, like an ever rolling stream, bears all its sons away," but on that occasion the son was rather young. It did not strike one so hard when older men passed away, but it seemed so often now that one had to address their worships on the passing away of sous of Warring- ton, more particularly from the Bench than from among the officials. In his friend, Luke Talbot, he was par- ticularly interested, seeing that he (Mr. Browne) was

he one twelve years ago to welcome him publicly at the Police Court when he was appointed in succession to the late jr.N S oriel Hunt. Since that time he and Talhot had been the most intimate friends. Mr. Talbot gave him all his confidences, and he (Mr. Browne) knew all his troubles and all his joys. Latterly it had been patent to all that his health had consider- ably broken down. But they.must not take the last few years as a pattern of those previous. He (Mr. Browne) could safely say there was no finer detective in England to-day than Mr. Talbot was in his time. There was no finer Chief Constable in his day than Luke Talbot was in the first few years he was in Warrington. He brought the force from a somewhat dilapidated con4ition into one of the finest, if not the finest, forces in England. He could say from the reports given by the Gevern- ment Insnector and from his own intimate knowledge of the force and its working, that there was no force of higher efficiency in England to-day than Warrington. Mr Talbot would go away; nothing would stop him. "Man proposes and God disnoses," and so they must take what God willed Their sympathies went out to his widow with every hope and wish that her future life might be blessed with the memory that her late husband was held in the highest esteem by the Public of Warring- ton. He ventured to hope that they saw his successor in Court. The feeling of the town was so great that there was no other name mentioned as his successor, hut one. He wished to associate himself with every- thing which had been said by the Mayor.

TRJBUTE BY ALDERMAN BENNETT. Speaking at the meeting of the Literary and Philosophical Society on Monday, Alderman BENNETT said he el-mid not refrain from briefly alluding to the recent tragic death, in a far-off land, of one of their best-known and ablest fellow-townsmen. That, was not the Place to Dv die trihnte to the public and official services of their late Chief Constable, and Mr. Talbot was not a member of their society; but he felt that, as their President, he should be sadly lacking in his duty if he did not make a passing reference, ere he quitted his post, to one whose literary gifts were not by any means the least of his endowments, and many of whose verses Warrington should not willingly let die. He thought of old John Fitchett, and of William Davies, and of many another local singer. but he doubted if anybody sines the days of fair L'etitia Aikin had sung in the old town so sweetly and so well. (Applause.) Luke Talbot was certainly a poet of no mean order, as all of them, he thought,would reldily admit. Their friend had not given them any of his verses in a collected and permanent fora:4lNA many of them were far too good to be left to the ephemeral glory of the magazines and newspapers. He ventured tmrohly to express the hope that some of the best of Mr. Talbot's poems might be garnered in a volume, and, it might be, handed on to generations just as far remote from them as they were from the singers and the scholars of the days of William Byres. That, at least, they owed to Mr. Talbot's memory. He would say no more, but, as still, for a brief hour or so, in some small sense responsible by his position as their President for the loving care of all their local literature, both past and present, he felt he could say no less. (Applause.)

JOURNALISTS' CONDOLENCE. At the annual meeting of the Warrington sub-district of the Tqstitute of Journalists, held sA the Lion Hotel on Saturday evening. references were made to the death of the Chief Constable, several members voicing the debt which Press rvresentatives owed to Mr. Talbot for his courtesy and consideration at all times. A vote of condolence was passed with Mrs. Talbot.

div.head: INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RECHABITES
div.p: INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RECHABITES
Warrington District No. 4.

A social evening of the members and friends of Charity tent No. 11, was held in the tent room, Friars Green school, Cairo-street on Tuesday. Bro. W. Wright tent secretary, presided and in his remarks spoke of the yeat 1908 as one of the most successful in the history of the tent for the last 20 years both from a numerical and financial standpoint. The membership of the tent at the end of the year 1906, was 183, this being a clear gain of 23 members during the year. They had also two strong Juvenile branches in connection witt• the adult tent which were doing a goad work amangst the children, and training them to become efficient members of the adult section. John Dimond juvenile tent had now over 200 members and Wycliffe juvenile tent about 1.30 members, a record that every officer and member ought to feel proud of. Songs were Riven in good style by Sisters T. MooreXiss E. Gallon,and Bro.W. Barton,and selections on the mandoline by Sister Isabella Broomhead.

Bro. W. Pharaoh, Deputy Ruler, was called upon through the absence of the Chief Ruler, Bro. J. H. Edwards, owing to sickness, to make a presentation of a framed emblem of the Order to Bro. Thomas Moore, Past Chief Ruler, and also a sash, with star and tassel, to Bro. George Ryder. Tent Steward.

Bro. PaA.fieoti, in his brief remarks, said it gave him great pleasure to present to Bro. Moore on behalf of the officers and members of the tent such a beautiful framed emblem as an appreciation of his services and work in passing through the various positions in the tent. Be also presented to Bro. George Ryder a Bath with star and tassel as a recognition of his valuable services for having introduced 12 new members in the tent during the year 1906, and hoped that many of the young mem- bers present would aspire to become officers of the tent. Bro. MOORE, in replying, said his heart was too full to express his thought and feelings to the officers and members of Charity Tent for their kindness in making him the presentation of a P.C.R. framed emblem. He was sure that his services were not worthy of such a Iconsideration. In filling the various offices of the Tent he considered he had been fully repaid by the kindness and courtesy that had been shown to him by the mem- bers during his term of oface, and should look back with pleasure npon the many happy recollections of the rent meetings. Although he was out of office he should in the future do all he could to promote total Abstinence, and extend the influence and blessing of the I Rechabite Order in our midst.

Bro. RYDER expressed his gratitude to the officers and members for the presentation of the sash as a recognition of any small services that he had been able to render to the tent during the year 1906 and hoped he should have strength given to him to use his influence to persuade young men to join an Order that was doing its very beat to destroy the drink curse, and ameliorate and uplift his fellowmen. Adult emblems duly filled in were also presented to eight members who had been transferred from the juveniles. Bro. THOS. LONGSRAW, D.D.R., Bro. C. S. FELLOWS, n.G.. and Bro. P. GANDY. hon. secretary of the Warrington and District Band of Hope Union, gave short addresses, and spoke of the good work being done from a temperance aspect by the Order of Rechabites. Refreshments were afterwards served, and full justice having been done to the good things provided it was the unanimous expression of all present that a splendid and profitable evening had been spent. A vote of thanks to the artistes and to the ladies for catering was proposed by Bro. D. HAMLETT and ssconded by Bro. E. LITTLE WOOD.

div.head: MISSIONARY PARLIAMENT.
div.p: MISSIONARY PARLIAMENT.

A Missionary Parliament was held last week in the Lecture Hall at Bewsey-road. The subject of deba/p was proYided by the recent revelations of atrocities in the Congo. Mr. John Upson, as Prime Minister, Moved the following resolution: "The Government regards the spiritual needs of Africa Nbrth of the Zambesi to be so pressing and important that it asks this House to raise snch additional funds as will establish new Mission Stations in many parts of that wide territory." In an impassioned speech the Premier gave his excellent reasons for laying this Bill before the House. He said that the African mind is easily impressed by religious influence, and that, especially in the North, Africa is rapidly becoming Mahomedan. He also reminded the meeting of the harm the white man has done in Africa by introducing the drink and slave trades, and therefore we owe the negroes the blessings of Christianity. His strongest point was that she presence of missionaries would reveal more fully the horrors perpetrated in the Dark Continent, and so make their continuation impossible in the face of strong publieopinion. An amendment to the resolution was moved by the leader of the Opposition. Mr. Nicholson of Owens' College, Manchester, as follows: " While offering no resistance to the raising of additional funds, we are of opinion that such funds should be utilised for the maintenance and development of our existing missions." in an able speech the Member for Madras pointed out that, though the African readily accepts religious instruction as he quickly looses his enthusiasm under adverse circumstances, and so is not so valuable an ally and convert as the Hiudoo, for instance, who takes longer to convert, but is aftorwards_more stable, and true to his Faith.He also showed that the money and time which had already been spent in India and China would be practically wasted if the prepared harvest there was not reaped, because of the removal of the labourers to other fields. On these grounds he opposed the new Bill as injudicious. Mr. Gill, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, secanded the resolution, and Mr. Norman, the Minister of Education supported his party. Mr. Gordon Pitt, the Member for Rhodesia, seconded the amendment. At first the voting was by acclamation, and the speaker —Rev. Sidney Pitt—declared for the opposition, but when a division was made the Govern- ment was found to retain a considerable numerical majority.

div.head: TETE EXA.IVITNER,
div.p: TETE EXA.IVITNER,
MARCH 16th 1907

Notices of motion relating TEIE SECTS AND to the second reading TETE SCHOOLS. of the Education (Special Religious Instruction) Bill are accumulating on the Order paper of the House Of Commons. Three members sitting on the Con- tlervative benches have given notice to move that the Bill shall be "read a second time on this day SIR months," which is tantamount to moving its rPjection, since it is presumed that six months from the day set down for the second reading the /Tome will not be in session. Lord ROBERT CECIL, Who shares the views of his brother, Lord HUGH .I.lbnd who is almost as incessant a debater as Sir tDERICK BANBURY, has a motion of a MOTO definite character. He seeks to get the House of ec)mmons to declare that no measure dealing with 1111100n5 instruction in public elementary schools can be regarded as satisfactory which does not !eecrd equal treatment to all forms of such luEtruction. There is considerable effrontery in Buell a motion, for the whole of the present diffi- "ltY has arisen out of the determination of extreme High Churchmen, when the last Govern- was in office, to sezure inequality of treatment in a manner beneficial to the Church Establishment. Mr. F. E. SMITH, "e. young Liverpool lawyer who made a rnaiden speech giving promise of a Parlia- 41:entary talent which has not since manifested ItEelf to the same degree, puts down a notice of a sßliting character. It declares "That this House declines to proceed with a Bill which is unpre cedented in its retrospective character,which seeks to destroy denominational schools by financial
pressure, which relieves one type of conscience at the expense of another, and which will dislocate and increase the cost of education in many
localities." Mr. SMITH cannot be congratulated °n the accuracy of his method of statement,

hut his motion has the merit of putting his own view of the question in the extremist form. Mr. LEWIS M.s.clvigs, whose intentions are much the same as those of Mr. SMITH, will Propose that no further legislation with regard to elUCatio/1 is desirable which fails to concede the 13,rineiple that ratepayers should be allowed to ad°eate their payments towards the maintenance, evillargement, or improvement of the class of schools "ich they desire to support. A proposal more ngehiously devised for making confusion worse Ac"founded could not well be imagined. Mr. 14cIvEs presumes, of course, that the religious question is a parents' question. Nothing that has t'llcee place since Mr. BALFOUR chose to throw Our nleatiOnal system into the melting pot has justi- M that view of the facts. There is one opponent of the Bill as it stands ' °Aa the Liberal side of the House. This is Mr. D. .4" THOMAS, who proposes to move that no amend- 4:lent of the Education Act, 1902, can be eon- ' B,idered satisfactory which only partially relieves 'oeal education authorities of the obligation to Provide public money for the maintenance of denominational schools. The motion is one with Ivhieh most good Liberals will sympathise, but, of ccmvse, it cannot be carried. Happy, indeed, .!°°llld be the political circumstances of the hour they would permit of the summary sweeping "ay of the denominational difficulty in the manner suggested. We have, however, to accommodate our minds to the fact that no auMmary settlement and no final settlement aat present possible. Rapid advance is, never- theless, being made towards an almost general acceptance of a completely undenorninational 8378tem of national education. This has been the °Tie good result of prolonged and embittered dis- !liatiion. The perverse unreasonableness of sacrific- !ng the interests of education to those of the sects beginning to be clearly perceived in quarters where a few years since no such enlightenment was likely to penetrate. Meanwhile the Govern- is bent on meeting the hard ease of the Laseive Resister, and it is improbable that even t fie llouse of Lords will stand in the way of the '..ineval of so cruel an injustice as it is now aureitted was created by Mr. BA.LFOrrIVEI Act.

The shock which the THE LATE CHIEF news of Mr. Luke Talbot's CONSTABLE, death at Cairo caused in Warrington was intensified by the information that filtered through this week. Liter telegrams revealed the sad fact that the late Chief Constable had terminated his existence by his own act, and that a verdict of" Suicide whilst , temporarily insane " had been returned by a jury lat the British Consular Court. It is twelve years !since Mr. Talbot came to Warrington as a young man with an exceptional record behind him. He succeeded a Chief Constable of the old school in the late Mr. S. Hunt, and a greater contrast not only bnl-ween men but methods could scarcely be imigined. Mr. Talbot at once effected important ro nrms,and very early won the respect and esteem of the men under him,ani that cordial feeling con- tinned to the end. It took the public longer to understand the new head of the police force, for he was a man with some personal eccentricities gave rise to a certain amount of prejudice. That, however, he soon lived down and the better ho became known and the more he was liked and respected. Those whocould claim friendship with thn late Mr. Talbot know that his martinet-like exterior concealed a warmth of temperament and .oirit of bonhomie quite out of the ordinary. He was a most kindly, courteous, and entertaining rn in, possessing unique and unlooked-for talents. Nnt only as an official, but as a man who loved to identified with the life of the town, Mr. Luke Ta)bot will be greatly missed. It is saddening to think that the holiday which it was hoped would fc,rtify a:weakened constitution ended in the:grave, and deep sympathy will be felt with Mrs. Talbot in the tragedy of her bereavement.

Not very long ago the THE CONGO. '7 Congo used to be considered as equivalent to the white inqt: s grave. To-day it would be much nearer the truth to say that the white man has made the (-Jingo into the black man's grave- King Leopold of the Belgians anti the blood-thirsty, rubber- hunting crew under his orders have done their best to make Christianity a bye-word and a laughing stock. They have sacrificed in twenty years some 15,000,000 lives in their insatiate pursuit of wealth--and rubber. The horrors of the Congo hive bean related frequently of late, but they need to be iterated again and again, before the Tiople and the Government of this country are awakened to the measure of their responsibility in the matter. Great Britain was one of the parties to granting King Leopold the Sovereignty of the Congo—a state as big as Europe minus Russia—and there is no excuse for tolerating a moment longer the abominable atrocities occurr:ng daily and with which the Government is well acquainted. We hope Sir Edward Grey will act promptly and firmly in the matter. Meanwhile the protest meeting held at Brick-street, on Thursday evening ought to be at once supple- mented by a Parr Hall demonstration backed by all the Christian communities in the town. The people are in earnest about this question. They only need their feelings directing along a reason- able line of action, and the Government must and will take heed.

However pronounced our UNEMPLOYMENT. national prosperity may be, we are perpetually faced, in a form more or less severe by the problem of unemployment. The number of unemployed is al ways considerable, without reckoning those who are unemployable. A correspondent of a con- temporary tells of a new invention which is expected, during the course of the next ten years, to displace from 200,000 to 300,000 men now employed in gas and water works. As the displacement may be expected to be gradual, many of these will no doubt find work, after more or less privation, in other employments ; but there will probably enough be a large surplus thrown into the ranks of the unemployed, without means and without, hope for the future; strong, capable men, willing to work, and with nothing to do. The greater their domestic burdens are, the more hopeless their case must be. Even those philanthropic, or semi-philanthropic' organisations which make emigration a part of their regular work can do nothing for men with families. For thr most part, they drain away the single men, leav- ing thos9 who are most helpless to heln themselves. It is really a brain-racking, heart-breaking problem which is thus presented. Emigration from the old country is not a process of relieving ourselves from anything that can properly be described ag surplus population. The surplus remains, and becomes a sediment ; and this painful condition of things cannot be changed except by such organisa- tion as has not hitherto been devised or attempted.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

The disclosures made by Mr. W. E. Harvey in the House of Commons with regard to the working hours of railway servants—some of whom are on duty for eighteen hours a day—suggest that when a terrible disaster occurs the wrong men are prosecuted. o o

There is a deficiency of .t 370 29. 2d. on the last year's accounts of the Warrington Grammar School which sum is, of course, made up by a grant from the Education Committee. The deficit is comparatively, small, and need not be the cause of any public con- cern.

* * * In the South of London two rival butchers display the following announcements : My fine pork sausages My gran d por k Gd. per lb. To pay more sausages are Sd. per lb. is to be robbed. To. pay less is to be
poisoned. Developments are awaited with interest. o . _ _ _

A committee has been appointed to consider the practicability of reviving the Lymm May Queen Festival. It was a matter of regret to a great many people in Warrington and district that last year the revels did not take place. There are very few of these picturesque survivals of byegone daya in the present utilitarian age, and it would be a pity if the Lymm festival were entirely abandoned. * * *

The en al of the variation-s played on the family name of Smith seems to have arrived at last. The plain Smith we have long known ; also the hyphenated Smith, the double-barrelled Smith, Bob-cab Smith, the German Schmidt. Smith masquerading as Smythe and Smijth, and the Smith that was pronounced Carring- ton ; now a Sydney school prize list arrives with St. Smith. The Sainted Smith surely exhausts the possibilities of the case.—" Sydney Bulletin."

The magnificent new yacht, the G-rainaig, in which the Duke and Duchess' of Westminster are just now cruising is the largest at sea, being quite as big as an ordinary liner. It is more sumptuously appointed than even the Royal yacht. The State rooms are immense, and possess every up-to-date luxury, includ- ing electric light, which is installed throughout the vessel. The duke and duchess, who are entertaining a large party on board, are not expected back to Eaton Hall until May, when a large house party will occupy the house for the Chester races. * *
No playing or singing in the street after a request has been made to desist. _ _

No street hawking or shouting. No noisy roundabouts or shows. No street fighting of animals. No improperly clad bathers. No orange peel on the pavements. No bulls near footpaths. These are bye-laws passed by the Merionethshire County Council in the effort to secure Paradise by legislation. • * * * An amusing story is this week told of a prominent "Heathen." On Saturday last owing to some failure one of the Corporation tram cars stopped when near the swing bridge and for half an hour refused to budge. The passengers naturally descended and. ,completed the journey on foot. Not so the old gentle- man. He bad paid the extra halfpenny for a ride to

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, March 16, 1907.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March 16, 1907.

Vietaria-square, he said, and he was go.ing to have his moneys' worth. With a dogged determination he sat on until the car again moved, and at the terminus alighted with an air of triumph and wended his way home. * * *

The Rev. J. F. Matthews' meetings for men termin- ated for the season on Thursday evening. Since the middle of October eighteen services have been held, and at least 500 men have listened to the addresses with deep interest. On Thursday evening at the close of Mr. Matthews' remarks, a nunaber of them expressed their appreciation of the helpfulness and practical Christianity found in the meetings and hoped they would be resumed next autumn. In all probability they will. Mr. Matthews has enjoyed the work, arduous though it has proved, and he my be relied upon to keep in touch as closely as possible with his new congregation. * *

The conclusion of the present series of popular penny concerts at Bold-street schools once more directs attention to the remarkable success which has attended the enterprise of the committee. Every Saturday evening for months past there have been crowded audiences, and it was estimated that the gathering at the last concert numbered over SOO. This is sufficient proof that the entertainments have filled a decided need in our town, and it is pleasing to find that the public really appreciate good concerts at a very nominal charge. A special word of praise is due to the Bev. J. Manning, the energetic originator of the project. * _ _

The members of Emmanuel Church are a go-a-head community. They have just purchased the line organ which is being removed from Bold-street Wesleyan Church to make a way for a more powerful instrument to be acquired at a cost of about £7OO. The affair was arranged as a pleasant little surprise for the minister (Rev. F. Vaughan) and on his return from his recent mission in London he was presented witn the receipt. In order that the instrument mly be installed, considerable structural alterations will have to be undertaken, so that more funds will be required. We believed, however, that the congregation will rise to the occasion an I realize the hops that when the new organ is opened the debt will have been cleared off.

* * * Now is the time to subscribe something towards the upkeep of the Warrington Children's Summer Camp. The camp has been extended and enlarged, and a lease of the ground has been secured for 14 years. Luly Greenall has defrayed the cost of an Assembly Room, and a number of huts now take the place of the former unhealthy tents. There is still a balance due to the Treasurer, and it is hoped that the people of Warring- ton will show their customary generosity towards a deserving object. Last summer no less than 53(1 Warrington children had a holiday at the camp, and there will be more this year if, as is hoped, funds permit. Subscriptions, however small or large may be sent to Mr. A. H. Lee, Brick-street, or Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, Bank Chambers, Winwick-street. • r, _ _ _

Les cloches de Buttermarket-street may or may not be a cause celebre in the law courts. Rumour says that the new peal of bells at Buttermarket-street sound very nice in the Catholic ear but create a horrible discord in the ears of those who worship opposite. The latter headed by Mr. Hetty Thornton,have protested vigorously against the ringing of the bells during the time of their morning service, and threats of legal proceedings are flying about. It is to be hoped that friendly counsels will prevail, and that some arrangement may be come to between the two parties. A quarter of an hour each way in altering the time of the respective services, it seems to us, would meet the difficulty. If it won't, then the clash of arms as well as of bells may be heard very soon. * *_

The report submitted by the School Nfanagernent Committee on the means for increasing the accommo- dation at the Secondary School and the Technical Institute is a model one from the point of view of the economist. The Committee has evidently tried to cut its coat according to the cloth available and this is a welcome departure from precedent in regard to these two buildings. Instead of an ambitious constructional scheme the Committee suggests making increased use of the Gymnasium at a very small cost for the purposes of the Secondary School, while the proposals for the Technical Institute embrace the provision of a mechnical laboratory, an engineers' workshop, and a drawing office on modest lines. The only new build- ing necessary will be an erection containing two floors, and ,for this a preliminary estimate is to be prepared. *

Councillor Stott, as an appreciation of his work as Trades Council Secretary for six years, was at the Trades Council meeting on Tuesday evening presented with a clock and bronzes. Messrs. Plumb, Podnaore, Haley, Plinston, Pook, Massey, and others spoke in glowing terms of the work done by the ',recipients and testified as to his zeal and enthusiasm for the cause .of trades unionism and labour while acting as secre- tary. Some of the speakers also referred to the fact that he was held in very high esteem 1.),i many members of the Town Council Niko are opposed to him in politics and a.zainst his Socialism. During his term of office the Trades Council has been more active and influential, that at any other period of its history. Councillor Stott in reply said that many times his words and actions had been misunderstood, but all he had said and done while acting as secretary had been in the interest of the Trade Union movement.

I Canon Scott Holland's Visit. ; Canon Scott Holland, of St. Paul's Cathedral, London, will visit Warrington on Sunday and address a service for men to be held at the Parish Church at three o'clock in the afternoon. In addition to being a very eloquent preacher, the Canon is well known as a stenuous social worker and is one of the ablest of Anglican Church leaders. Accident to an Office aoy. A peculiar accident happened to an office boy at Messrs. Crosfield's yeste •day. ale was using a copy- ing press when he pulled it from its stand, with the result that it fell on his foot and crushed it badly. The boy's name is 'Arthur Lythgoe (16), of 70, Mancheiter-road. He was taken to the Infirmary and ' detained. Animated Pictures. This week kir. Carter's New Century Pictures con- clude a fortnight's visit to Warringt In. The proceed- ings have been highly successful and the shows have nightly been watched by crowded houses in the Parr Hall. Last week's pictures were in every way excel- lent and on Monday the programme was completely changed and the pictures were if anything finer than _ ever. The last performances will be given to-day at 3 p.m. and S p.m. Sad Burning Fatality.. • An inquest was held at Warrington yesterday on the body of Thomas Pridden, the two-year old son of Thomas Pridden, 11, Golborne-street,who died in the Infirmary on Wednesday from burns received earlier in the day. It transpired that the child was left alone in the house and that the fire was not in any way guarded. Mr. Brighouse said he hoped that the Bill . with reference to the provision of fire-guards, at present before the House of Commons,would shortly become law.—A verdict of " Accidental death" was , returned.

div.head: WARRINGTON
div.p: WARRINGTON

Mr. B. H. Pearce will hold his first annual concert in Bold-street Wesleyan schools on Monday evening when an exceptionally attractive programme will be presented. A Shop Assistants' and Labour demonstration to pratest against radius agreements will be held in Bold-street schools on Tuesday evenng when Mr. H. L. Barrett, shop assistants' organiser, will deliver an address. At the meetings of the Spiritual Saciety to-morrow (Sunday) afternoon and evening, Mr. W. Rooke will speak. On Monday evening there will be a public tea, follewed by an interesting entertainment.

Meeting of Teachers. A largely-attended meeting of Warrington teachers was held at the Town Hall last evening, when an interesting address on important educati,mal topics was delivered by Mr. A. R. Smith, Chief Inspector for the district.

A Local Invention. We give below a description of a recent patent application, contributed by Messrs. Howard and Co., Patent Agents, 57 and 58, Chancery-lane, London, W.C. Complete specification.-21,55.2, Lubricators, K. E. Markel, and H. Roberts, both of Bank Quay, Warrington, Lancashire :—A railway axle-box is lubricated by rings placed over the journal and fitting in grooves in the bearing. The rings have knife-edges at the sides to reduce friction in the grooves and perforations to cariy oil. Tradesmen's Association. The quarterly general meeting of the Warrington Tradesmen's Association was held in Messrs. Toft's Assembly Room, Bridge-street, on Tuesday evening, Mr. W. Roberts, occupying the chair. There was some discussion on the question of street lighting, but the principal item was the question of the guardian's elections. Joint sub-commipees of the Tradesmen's Association and the Property Owners' Association had met on several occasions, and their report as to the candidates recommended for support was laid before the meeting and after considerable debate was adopted. The matter of the collection of shop refuse and the charge made for such collection by the Corporation was brought forward and the feeling of the meeting ' was that this charge was a most unfair one, but the subject *as referred to the Executive Committee to deal with. The Rev. Charles M. Sheldon.

-- The coming visit to this country of the Rev. Charles M. Sheldon, of Topeka, Kansas, U.S.A., author of "in Hig Steps" and many other books, is being looked forward to with great interest by Christian and temperance workers ; act only by those who heard him when he visited this country a few years ago, but by those who only know him tw his writings. Mr. Sheldon's visit will be of short duration, as he is due it Australia by the middle of July for engagements ihere. The campaign which he is undertaking on tehalf of the United Kingdom Alliance will commence bith a special service in the historic Free Trade Hall, wanchester, on Sunday evening, 24th inst. Afterwards Mr. Sheldon will address meetings in many other places. He will speak at Wycliffe Church on Monday Mardi 25th In view of the coming Licensing Bill, Mr. Sheldon's visit is regarded as most timely. He has much valuable information to impart on the stab- ject of local prohibition in America.

div.p: GUARDIANS ELECTIONS.
SIX CONTESTS IN WARRINGTON.

The number of candidates for seats on the Warring- ! ton Board of Gnardians has not been materially reduced by reason of withdrawals, and in six out of the ten Warrington wards contests will take place. In Orford Ward Mr. W. McNeil Sloane has retired from the field and Mrs. Wilkinson. therefore resumes her seat on the Board unopposed. A three-cornered contest was promised in Latchford but the withdrawal , of the Rev. J. F. Matthews reduces the number of con- testants. Mrs. Osborne, whose retirement from St. John's Ward we announced last week, has also retired from St. Austin's (No. 2) Ward. In the outside dis- tricts the representation of Houghton, Middleton and ...krbury, has undergone a change Mr. J. W. Knowles having allowed Mr. Stanier to be returned unopposed. In Burtonwood Mr. Richard Forshaw, after a prospect of a stiff fight, has been left alone in the field, his opponents Messrs. William Fairclough and Thomas , Dutton having retired. The Wards in which contests , will take place, together with a list of the candidates are : -
ST. AUSTIN'S, NO. 2. William Throssell, 676, Knutsford-road, gentleman,and Rev. M. Ryan, 7, Liverpool-road.

Mr. Dobson, district coroner, held an inquiry at the Runaorn Court House on Monday, into the circum- stances attending the death of Joseph McVeigh, a sea- man on the s.s. Cheshire, who died on Saturday from injuries received the same morning while the vessel was moored at the Old Quay. Mr. W. Shaw, senr., was fore- man of the jury. Mr. Taylor, solicitor, and Captain Heasley appeared for the Ship banal Company, and Mr. Heyne (Messrs. Hill, Dixon and Co.) represented the owners, Messrs. J. J. Mack and Co., Liverpool.—Antony Johannesen, a Swede, living in Belfast, said he was second mate on the s.s. Cheshire belonging to Messrs. J. J. Mack and Sons. The deceased lived at 18, Vulcan- street, Belfast. On Saturday morning they were getting ready to leave the Old Quay about five minutes past four. Deceased was standing on the port side aft and witness was amidships by the capstan. The pilot sang out "Is all clear aft ?" He (witness) replied in the affirmative. A man named ,Thomas Shaw was letting go the stern-rope and witness was hauling the rope on the vessel. Deceased was standing by the other rope on the port side. Unfortunately deceased got a bit of the rope round his leg, and was carried half round. Lie shouted that his leg was jammed and witness called out to the pilot to put fall steam astern and that was done at once. Deceased said his leg was off altogether. Witness helped him into the mess roorn,and he was subsequently conveyed on the ambulance to the hospital.—The Coroner: Was deceased in a place where he had to be? —Witness: Yes,sir.—ln answer to the Foreman,witness said the ship would go aft about twenty yards before ! the capstan could stop.—lsahel Jane Wallace, matron at the Cottage Hospital, said the deceased was admitted at ; a quarter past five on Saturday morning. His leg had I been torn off between the knee and the thigh. He died lat ten minutes past ten the same morning. He suffered great pain.
