div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
WIDNES POLICE SERGEANT HONOURED.

The Chief Constable of Lancashire, on the recom- mendation of Superintendent Strickland, has awarded Sergeant Herbert Whitehead the "merit" badge, in recognition of special services rendered by that officer in connection with a recent assize case. Sergeant Whitehead, who has been stationed in Widnes for four years, is a highly respected and efficient officer. RUNCORN'S PASSIVE RESISTER.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Messrs. A. Thomas and W. Timmis, Mr. R. H. Posnett, ' The Mount, Runcorn, was summonned for non-payment lof a portion of the poor rate. He did not appear. Mr. W. Sutton said the rate was £3 16s. 7d. and Mr. Posnett Ihad paid £3 16s. This was the only case of passive resistance. Last half-year all of them paid. An order was made for immediate payment. 1 ' _ COAL THEFT AT WIDNES.

At the Widnes Police Court on Monday, before the May Alderman S. Owens and Councillor F. Neil,James Nolan, of Catherine-street, was charged with having stolen 1171 b. of coal, value is. 3d., from the Widnes Foundry Company's yard at 11.45 p.m. on the Bth March. He pleaded guilty.—Superintendent Strickland said that in consequence of complaints made by the Widnes Foundry Company regarding thefts of coal Police-Constable Jones and Dickenson were on duty, in plain clothes, at the Bridge and Girder Works of the Foundry Company on the date in question. They saw the prisoner and another man, at 11.45. p.m., fill a bag with coal. They seized the prisoner, but the other man decamped. Owing to the darkness and the state of the yard chase proved futile. When Nolan was charged at the Police Station he made no reply.—Prisoner remarked that he had nothing to say.—The Mayor said the Conditions under which the offence had been committed aggravated it. Prisoner would be fined 40s. and costs or a month's imprisonment. RUNCORN MAN'S NARROW ESCAPE.

j The story of how a Runcorn man nearly lost his life at Chester was told at the Chester Cily Police Court, 1 on Monday, before the Mayor (Alderman J. Jones) and 1 Colonel Evans-Lloyd, when William Brough, of 54. Bentinck-street, Runcorn, described as an engine driver for one of the Runcorn manufacturing firms, was charged with being drunk and disorderlyat the Chester General Railway Station on Saturday night, and also with assaulting Detective Brooks, in the employ of the Railway Company.—Prisoner pleaded guilty to the first charge, but said he could not remember the assault.— Mr. Fenno, who prosecuted on behalf of the Railway Company, said on Saturday night prisoner was in such a 1 drunken condition on the platform that !mien on to 1 the line, along which the Birkenhead train was coming into the station. He was assisted on to the platform, Ibut he again fell, and he was taken out of the station. Prisoner returned and created a disturbance by wanting Ito fight anybody who was in the road around him. Detective Brooks and Constable William then took hold of him to take him into custody, but he tripped them up, and after kicking Brooks in the eye assaulted Williams badly.- -John Ratcliffe assistant stationmaster. corroborated, and said that when the prisoner fell on to the line it took four or five other passengers to get him on to the platform again, while others ran forward and waved their arms to stop the train.—Prisoner said he was told to go that way, and he was very sorry for what he had done. It was the first time he had been in a police court in his life, and he did not recollect striking the detective. He fancied the injury to the detective's eye I was done by the fall—The Mayor said the prisoner !would have to go to gaol for a month in each case, the sentences to run concurrently. 1 SAILOR'S LEG TORN OF?.

div.head: "SHAM CLOTH HAWKERS."
div.p: "SHAM CLOTH HAWKERS."

Alfred Tansley, of 2, Redburn-street, Liverpool, and Henry Beachill, 71, Howard-street, Liverpool, were remanded at St. Helens on Wednesday on charges of acting as pedlars without certificates, and also with lattempting to obtain money by false pretences. The [Chief Constable said the men were arrested at Sutton the previous day by Sergeant Stewart. He alleged that they were members of a gang that were known as the "sham cloth hawkers." They went out fro Liver- pool to different districts, and, after distri m buting bills which stated that a sale of cloth and other goods was , to take place, they went round with genuine samples on which they took orders which were never executed; and they also took some of the cheapest cloth they could buy. In one of the cases cloth which was not worth more than 12s. was offered for 355. and the woman WAS told that it was worth 655. Another charge had been unearthed that morning, and he asked for a remand until Saturday.—The bench agreed.

div.head: LICENSING SESSIONS.
div.p: LICENSING SESSIONS.

At the St. Helens Licensing Transfer Sessions, on Monday, the bench granted the transfer of the Engine and Tender, Reginald-road, Sutton. from Ralph Fenney to William S. Garton, farmer, of Bold.—The proposed enlargement of the New Market Inn, Naylor-street, was asked for by Mr. Kelly, who offered, on behalf of Messrs. George Shaw and Co., of Leigh, to surrender the licences of the Baths Hotel, Warrington New-road. and the Nancy Hotel, Pocket Nook. The bench had asked for some domestic accommodation to be provided on the ground floor, but the owners claimed that this was impossible.—Mr.llaslam Fox,for the police,opposed the proposal to dispense with domestic compensation on the ground floor, the premises not being so well looked after as they might be.—Mr. T. Silk Wilson, of Manchester, the agent for the Society of Friends, presented an appeal to the bench not to accede to the proposal that was made for the enlargement of the house.—The bench retired, and aft 3r calling in Mr. Shaw and Mr. Kelly for consultation, they returned to the bench, it being understood that the magistrates refused to sanction the alterations suggested, and that they would treat the licence under the compensation clauses.—The objection to the renewal of the Baths Hotel, owned by the same flrm,was gone into by Mr. Fox. Inspector Goodall said there were four fully- licensed houses at this point, and only nine inhabitated houses between thern.—The bench decided to report for compensation all of the three bouses.—ln respect to the Nancy Hotel, evidence was given that the wife of the landlord was concerned in a wake kept up on the body of a child for a week. A great deal of drinking took place, and, it was alleged, that the landlady carried liquor to the house where the wake was held, ;,1

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON:
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON:
DROWNING FATALITY.

On Sunday afternoon a boy named Harold Smith, of 52, Regent-street, Earlestown, son of William Smith,was drowned whilst attempting to cross the bridge of the St. Helens Canal running through Earlestown. His body was recovered shortly afterwards. The deceased was nine years of age. GILCEIRIST LECTURES.

The fifth lecture was held in the Town Hall on Mon- day evening, the lecturer being Dr. Alex Hill, Master of Downing College, Cambridge. The subject was "The brains and minds of animals," and it was illustrated by limelight views. The Chairman, Mr. C. R. Pilkington, in introducing the lecturer spoke of the benefit the lectures were to th 3 people, especially to young people. OCCASIOSAL COURT.

At the Occasional Court, on Saturday, before Mr. T. Ormand, Joseph Kennedy and Keys Andentas were fined 2s. Gd. and costs each for being drunk and disorderly. Both are Poles residing'inAthol-street.—Edward Single- ton, of Earlestown, was charged with sleeping on the premises of the Bottle Works without visible means of support, and was committed to Strangeways gaol for 14 days. P.C. Knott proved the case. WESLEYAN DAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.

The annual services in co,mection with the above were held on Sunday, the preacher, morning and after- noon being the Rev. S. C. Hall, aud evening, Mr. W. Goslin. The children's singing,under the conductorship of Mr. W. Blackwell, was excellent. At each service a report was read out, of the progress the scholars had made, the course of instruction in addition to ordinary subjects being French, algebra, euclid, chemistry, electricity, magnetism, brush and water colour drawing, and lessons on health. The County Council Exhibition had been gained during the year. Essiys had been sent in by the upper standards, after the visit of the Lecturer of the Lancashire and Cheshire Band of Hope and Temperance Union. The examiner's remarks were as follows :—" The reports are complete and _very intelligent ; 111 certificates were awarded. Over 75 of the candidates scored 80 and more marks out of a possible 100, which must speak well for Mr. Burgess and his staff." The day's collections realized £l2 ss. 9d. PHYSICAL DRILL EXHIBITION.

The Vulcan Physical Drill Class held their annual entertainm3nt in the Town Hall on Saturday evening, when the chair was taken by their President, Mr. W. Collingwood. The juniors had a dumb bell competition, a club's competition, a bar balls competitions, and a free movements' competition and dumb bell race. D. Wright was first with a total or 39 points, R. Bennett second with 28 points, and .T. Bamford third with 37 points. The winners in the senior members' division in the club's competition and free movements were—S. Tomlinson, total 79 points; F. Pindar, 78 points ; W. Tarbuck, 73 points. The winner of the final iilnmb bell race for junior members was T. Lee. A gymnastic exhibition was given by members of the Balfour Insti- tute, Liverpool. Songs were given by Miss L. Barr, Mr. A. H. Hill, and the Brunswick Male Quartette Party. The judges were, ALessrs. Honey,Gaze and Davies,of the Balfour Institute, Liverpool. The medals were pre- sented by Mrs. Collingwood, each recipient being heartily applauded. The accorunanists were Messrs. W. Pearson and W. Taylor.

div.head: VOICE OF LABOUR.
div.p: THE VOICE OF LABOUR.
Edited by John Workman.

Reader:: of this column arc invited to assist in, making it- interesting and helpful to social workers by contributing themselves. Correspondents must write on one side of the paper only, and endeavour to ,nbake their letters and notes short and to the point. A nom-de-plume may be used, but the real name of the writer should be forwarded in confidence to thc Editor of the column. M.S.S. must be addressed to John. Workman, " Examiner " Office, Warrington and should be sent in not later than Wednesday in each week.

div.head: FAT a WAGES.
div.p: FAT a WAGES.

After many years of agitation by the Lancashire and Cheshire Federation, the Lancashire County Council have at last adopted the " Fair Wages " clauses approved by the Federation This is a splendid victory for trades unionism and proves the value of organised effort.

div.head: UNITY WANTED.
div.p: UNITY WANTED.

What has become of the unification scheme initiated by the Trades Council and considered by them during last year? We trust that the matter has not been allowed to drop. There is great need for action on the lines suggested for it cannot be said that Labour is at all adequately represented on the Town Council or Board of Guardians. It is to be hoped that the pioneers of the movement will keep up their agitation until there is a real live labour organisation sufficiently ' representative to obtain that representation on those public bodies to which the workers are entitled.

div.head: RAILWAYS.
div.p: THE RAILWAYS.

It has been said that the English are a nation of shopkeepers and certain it is that they pay frequent homage at the shrine of the G-od of Trade and rever- ence the mystic letters S. D. Perhaps it was this virtue, or weakness, call it what you will, that caused so much interest to be taken in the pinchbeck proposals for the consolidation of the Empire and the fossil remedies for our social ills that so recently emanated from a certain gieat city in the Midlands. People were told, and many believed it, that trade,our tradeovas being ruined by Machiavellian machinations of our organ-grinding, ice-cream vending or Sauer-kraut eating foes in other lands, and that the only remedies for the ills of our body politic were the Tariff Tonic and the Pills of Protection. The public however placed no faith in the "Fakirs" but as the villain says, "There'll come a time, ah ! ah !" and true it is that we shall see the raging tearing propaganda of Protection again in full swing when the occasion is ripe and the times warrant. Do these dormant disciples of Tariff Reform ever realise that the problem of foreign competition is not wholly contained in the tariff question? Do they ever consider how British industry is taxed by— British Capitalists! many of whom are clamourous for Tariff Reform? Yet nothing is more in harmony with the eternal verities than this statement. "The British railways impose a tax on British industry and encomage foreign competition by the preferential character of their 'through rates." Corn comes from the heart of Canada to Liverpool and i then forwarded to London by rail and the total cost of carriage is less than the carriage of corn from Cheshire to London. This is a tax on the Cheshire farmer to the advantage of his Canadian competitor. Next week I will endeavour to show how other trades and occupa- tions suffer and prove to the hilt my statement that trade is fettered and agriculture crippled by the iniquitous railway rates which are made in the interest of the shareholder and, apparently, the foreigner.—STANLEY Loan.

div.head: PHYSICAL E;ETERIORATION.
div.p: PHYSICAL E;ETERIORATION.

Some time ago a State Department issued a report of a Committee on Physical Deterioration. The Com- mittee faced facts, investigated causes, and suggested remedies with a directness and celerity worthy of the ;laps in time of war. The Report records an investigation full of serious revelations of the ravages wrought by overcrowding, poverty, ignorance and drink. It is full of promise, also, by reason of the broad views taken of the situa- tion, and the practicahility of the remedies the Committee suggest. The inquiry calls for our individual attention—in our own persons—and for our attention collectively—in our political, social and industrial relations.

Individual self-restraint and .personal endeavour are called for. The Committee remark, "The people perish for lack of knowledge. Laziness, want of thrift, ignorance of household management, indiffer- ence to parental obligations, drunkenness, infect adults lof both sexes and press with terrible severity upon their children. "Personal as well as social reform is evi- dently requisite; but betterment of environment,human- i zing of conditions of employment, housing reform,an d generally increased facilities of healthy recreation and enjoyment, are still mire necessary. Mr. Balfour, I believe, attributed intemperance among the masses to their double inheritance of depravity. Presumably the workers received an extra serving of original sin. The Committee on Physical Deteri:lration state the poor err because they inherit not king. I quote again "The poor often drink to get the effects of a good meal; they mistake the feeling of stimulation after alcohol for the feeling of nutrition." Dr. Eicholz, whose evidence the Committee endorses, states that outside the hereditary diseases which affect poor and well-to-do alike there is little evidence of a pre-natal character to account for the widespread physical degeneracy of the poorer population. He says "There is accordingly every reason to anticipate rapid amelioration of physique when an improvement occurs in external conditions, particularly as regards food, clothing, overcrowding." In fact all evidence points to active, rapid improve- ment bodily and mental in the worst districts so soon as they are exposed to better circumstances.. The report generally goes to show that physical deterioration is largely due to the vile conditions of social and industrial life which are with us to-day.— The future is with the Democracy —an intelligent, virile and educated Democracy —prepared to use its power in order to socialise the means of life. Forward, comrades—the day dawns.—LAzArtus.

STEAM POWER. One of the most striking characteristics of the past has been the continual and steady increase in the use of steam power and labour saving machinery in the industries both of this country and also every other great manufacturing nation. Along with this increase of power has gone on an increase of efficiency in the application of that power to human uses, so that pro- bably each horse or man-power now employed in this country in the countless forms of wealth is at least ten times as efficient as it was a century ago. The railroad train has taken the place of coach and wagon, the steamship of the sailing vessel, the scythe and the flail have, to a large extent, been superseded by reap- and threshing machines, dozen of pairs of boots and shoes can now be turned out with less labour than an old-fashioned cobbler could have put on a sole,and in the modern factory cotton becomes cloth faster, with a girl attendant, than could have been turned out by scores of weavers with their handlooms, whilst the utilization of the wonderful powers of electricity (telegraph, telephone, traction &c.,) and the various applications of modern science to the arts and indus- tries have economised both time and labour. Bat the enormous power of machinery and man's increased control of the forces of nature have not, as might reasonably have been anticipated, appreciably lessened the toil of the workers or removed poverty, pauperism and destitution from our midst. Every part of the civilized world is subject to recur- ring 'periods of severe trade depression when labour is condemned to involuntary idleness and large masses of the people are unable to secure even the bare necessaries of a decent human life. This lamentable state of things is common both to those couutries where there is an autocratic government and where political power is vested in the people, also where protective tariffs are enforced and where so-called Free Trade prevails whilst these deplorable social i evils are prevalent n those communities where large standing armies are maintained and also where the standing army is merely nominal. One man owns a il machine w,ich does work previously performed by Th 500 men. e one man thus secures the product of that machi▪ ne and therefore has .practically 500 times as much income as he formerly received 'which is now probably a great deal more than he really needs. On the other hand 300 men are thrown out of employment and there i , i s something tragic in the fact that as soon as a machi▪ ne s invented to do his work man begins to starve. Were that machine the property of all everyone would benefit by it and thus it would be an immense advantage to the community. lit present machinery competes against man but in a properly ' regulated State machinery would be the servant of man and not man the slave of machinery as is so prevalent under existing industrial conditions.— ° WEN ROBERT.

div.head: WARRINGTON
div.p: WARRINGTON

The New Post Office The Lords of the Treasury have sanctioned the expenditure by the Office of Works during the coming year of £7,500 on the new Post Office at Warrington (in addition to £6,500 already expended; total estimated cost £15,900). An incorrigible Character. James Leonardy, of Rose and Crown-street, War- rington, who was described by Superintendent Monaghan, at the Police Court on Monday, us an incorrigible and dangerous character, was sent to gaol for one month with hard labour for being drunk and disorderly and assaulting Police-constable Andrews. Ship Canal Bill. The King, in his capAcity a.:4 the Duke of Lancaster. has given his consent to the van 'us powers bill of the Manchester Ship Canal Co, which, amongst other things gives power to pump in additional water, with a view of deepening the waterway. The bill has been reported to the House of Lords, with amendments, and now awaits the third reading before being sent to the House of Commons.

IPUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST 1 BOOTS IN LANCA.SHIR.E.—Advt. , I Tableaux at Bewsey-road. I Interesting entertainments were provided at . Bewsey-road Lecture Hall last week-end, the proceeds ' being in aid of the bazaar fund. A. series of tableaux I were given by some of the young people connected j with the Wesleyan Church and included scenes from ! " Othello " and " The Sign of the Cross," and repre- sentations of " Where are you going to, my pretty maid ?" " The Gambler's wife," " Blind beggars," : " Love, courtship and marriage," concluding with a i patriotic tableau. There were large audiences and the entertainments,which/were exceedingly creditable, were much enjoyed. A. substantial sum wtis realized. Spiritualist Anniversary. The tenth anniversary of the Warrington Spirit- ! ualist Society was celebrated on Sunday when special! meetings were held in the Druids' Hall. The speaker i was Miss Ruth Sage, a young lady who is very popular among Spiritualists, and there were exceed- i ingly good audiences to meet her. On Sunday afternoon her subject was "The work of religion." In the evening the President gave a rief resume of the career of the society, and Miss Sage delivered an address on " The power of Spiritualism," pointing out that its power lay in the fact that it stepped in where other systems of religion failed,and undoubtedly demonstrated the fact that our " dead" are still living and are not far removed from us. On Monday night the hall was again filled, and Miss Sage gave a short address on ".The freedom of Spiritualism." At each meeting there were clairvoyant delineations. 1 PUBLIC BENEFIT, UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCA.SHIRE.—Advt. 1 1 Swimming Club Annual Meeting. 1 The annual meeting of the Warrington Swimming i Club was held at the Corporation Baths on Monday evening, Mr. E. Diapei presiding over a small attend- ance.—ln his annual report the Searetary expressed the hope that this year the water polo team would be more successful. The balance sheet showed that the club was in a flourishing position, the year opening with a credit balance of £33 and closing with a balance in hand of £4l 10s.—The Mayor was . elected president, the vice-presidents being re-elected with the addition of the name of Mr. F. J. Lord. Other elections were : Treasurer, Mr. S. Walker ; secretary, Mr. J. N. Vernon; assistant secretary, Mr. C. Newton ; captain, Mr. C. Wood; sub-captain, Mr. R. Allen ; committee, Messrs. E. Draper, A. Barlow, F. Garsicle, A. Boscoe,R. Harding, C. H. Wood, J. Newton, S. Roberts and D. Wright ; delegate to the N.C.A.S.A., &c. Mr. J. N. Vernon; auditors, Messrs. F. Garside and R. Harding. Votes ! of thanks to retiring officers concluded the meeting. I Presentation at Cockhedge Mills. A very pleasigg incident took place at Cockhedge Mills on Wednesday night, when Mr. Henry Kirk received from his fellow-workmen a presentation in commemoration of his retirement. Mr. Henry Kirk, who has worked at Cockhedge Mills for over 50 years, received from the hands of Mrs Wilson on behalf of a few of his fellow-workmen a handsome p..esent in the form of a comfortable arm chair, long pipe, and tobacco jar filled with tobacco' also a pouch with silver-mounted plate, bearing the following inscrip- tion : "Presented to Mr. H. Kirk from a few of his friends from Cockhedge Mills." Mr. Wilson, in pre- senting the above, remarked on the pleasure it gave him to perform such a pleasant duty and hoped Mr. Kirk would be spared a long time yet to enjoy the comfort and pleasure of such service- able presents. Messrs. J. Taylor, T. Lurner, and W. Bridge also made suitable remarks on the occasion. Mr. Kirk responded with many thanks for the kind manner in which they had appreciated him and hoped be would long be spared to enjoy the use of their gifts. The workmen then joined in with the clapping of hands and wished him good health. LADIES' BEST GLACE Bocrrs AND SHOES, UNDER THE CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—Adtv. Popular Penny Concerts. The last of the popular penny concerts in the Bold- street Schbols was given on Saturday evening. The series has been surprisingly successful and again there was a crowded attendance. The artistes were : Miss Watkins, Miss Stronach, Mr. W. Clare,,Mr. R. A. Robinson, Mr. Dan Johnson (humorist), and Miss Profit (instrumentalist). Voealists and instrumentalist acquitted themselves in a very praiseworthy manner, and the performance was in every way excellent. During an interval in the programme Councillor Hoddart, of Salford, and the Rev. J.Manning delivered addresses, the last-named speaking in high terms of the services of the Hon. See. (Mr. E. Pliuston), Mr. Frank Hickman, Mr. Tom B rough, Mr. Walter Brough, Mrs. Prince, caretaker, and the artistes. He hoped that next season the concerts would be still more successful. Similar concerts to these had been carried on for 18 years in Manchester, and 2,000 people were present each Saturday night. When these concerts were starte3 it was said they would collapse in a few months, but he was pleased to be able to state that the prophets had not proved correct. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He hoped this movement would prove the beginning of a bigger one by which they would honestly try to keep into closer touch with the life of the people of the town. (Applause.) He was sorry he should not be present to see the success of next year's gatherings, as he would leave Warrington at the end of August,-but he hoped as he had already said, they would continue to increase in popularity. (Applause. Prior to the conclusion of the concert, the secretary, on behalf of the committee, spoke of the debt of gratitude which all owed t the Rev. J. IManning, who inaugurated the concerts, and who had superintended them throughout. , The Butt Concert. We would remind our readers that Madame Clara Butt and Mr. Kennerley Rumford and party will give a concert in the Parr Hall on Wednesday next. Particular interest centres in the event,as these great vocalists will make their last appearance in Warrington previous to their departure for a tour round the world, from which they will not return to this country until some time in 19.08, and cannot therefore appear again in the provinces until the season 1908-1909. Madame Clara Butt and Mr. Kenietfey Rumford will come fresh from laurels gained in some of the leading provincial towns and cities. In fact -to quote the wdrds of one who was present at the Liverpool concert a few days ago —it was "a great triumph ; Mdme. Butt sang gloriously, as also did Mr. Rumford. £425 house —record of the season; hundreds turned away." Seats are being rapidly booked for the Warrington concert, but a number of tickets are still on sale for all parts of the hall st Mr. R. H. Pearson's, 75, Bridge- street. It is interesting to rote that Madame Butt has recently given a writer somi, views on singing in English. She says : " The general public want more sentiment than art ; and a little sacrifice of one's testhetic principles for wider and more sympathetic ones not only binds one closer to the hearts of one's listeners, but opens to them a new field of musical enjoyment. Our language is a beautiful one to sing in, if only young vocalists gave the same trouble to its pronounciation as they do to that of songs, say in Italian, which they will study syllable by syllable with experts." An admirable programme has been arranged for ' Wednesday's concert. Madame Butt will sing the aria " Divinites du Styx" (Gluck), a new song (by S. Liddle the composer of "Abide with me") "Eastertide" (accompanied by the composer on the organ) and the song" Smiles" (K. Heron-Maxwell). Mr. Kennerley Rumford will contribute three delightful songs, and the other members of the party are Mjss Edith Evans (the new soprano), Mr. Philip Simmons (tenor, of Paris), Mr. Ilia Mossel (the famous Dutch violinist), Mons Hollnian (the world-famous 'cellist who will play on a 1,000 guinea 'cello), Mr. S. Liddle, the famous composer of "Abide with me "(conductor), and Mr. P.-Mayon Ibbs (piano.)

div.p: The Examiner, SPturday, March 16, 1907. OF INTEREST TO MOTHERS.

Personal. Mr. Basil McG..rty, son of Lieut. McGarty, formerly of Warrington, now residing at, Blackpool, passed the Lond University Matriculation examination held in January last. Mr. Basil McGarty who studied without , professional assistance received his eally education at the Warrington People's College and earned the Grammar School Scholarship from t e above school. Mrs. Simpson of Bewsev-road has been appointed a member of the National Executive of the British Women's Temperance Association. PREMIER CYCLES with k,turmey Archer three speed gear, nine guineas. wo speed gear eight guineas.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. South Lancashires' Band for France. Colonel F. A. Adam, commanding the 2nd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, now forming part of the Aldershot Army Corps, has given his consent to the , fine band of the regiment accepting a very pressing invitation to visit Lille next month. The number of ! occasions upon which a British military band has played on the Continent during the past fifty years could almost be counted on the fingers of one hand, so that this honour is all the more to be prized. Concert by Messrs. Crosfield's Band. A large attendance assembled in the works dining hall at Bank Quay on Saturday ,evening when an 'enjoyable concert was given by the above band in a manner which promises well for the success of the ' band during the coming contest season. Various items I were given. The selection for the New Brighton Tower contest was rendered in a masterly style. Miss E. Barnes sang two songs, and was encored, as was Mr. E. Pownall,whose rich bass voice was heard to advan- tage in the descriptive song, "The desert." Mr. Norman Mosse pleased the audience with his ability on the violin. The band has been engaged to give two concerts at St. Helens in the Theatre and Opera House. BABY CARRIAGES.—New and exclusive designs now showing.—J. S. GARLAND, 51, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Tradesmen's Association. The quarterly general meeting of the Warrington Tradesmen's Association was held iu Messrs. Tuft's 'Assembly Room, Bridge-street, on Tuesday evening, Mr. W. Roberts, occupying the chair. There was some discussion on the question of street lighting, but the principal item was the question of the guardian's elections. Joint sub-cotnruittees of the Tradesmen's Association and the Property Owners' Association had met on several occasions, and their report as to the candidates recommended for support was laid before the meeting and after considerable debate was adopted. The matter of the collection of shop refuse and the charge made for such collection by the Corporation , was brought forward and the feeling of the meeting I was that ;his charge was a most unfair one, but the , subject was referred to the Executive Committee to I deal with. I Furious Motoring at Stretton At Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday, George John William Robertson, motor car driver, Grimsditch Hall, Whitley, was summoned for driving a motor car at a dangerous speed along London-road, Stretton, at 11.25 a.m. on February 23rd. Acting-Sergeant Kennerley stated that he was in plain clothes riding a bicycle at Stretton at the time in question, when defendant came along driving a motor car at a speed •of about 35 miles an hour. Defendant said he was only going at the rate of 20 miles an hour when he passed the witness. He blew his horn when he reached the cross roads. He admitted that he had been fined for a similar offence at Chester Castle, Liverpool and Birkenhead, the fine at the latter place amounting to £lO. He was now fined £1 and costs. UNDER THE CLOCK for Good BOOTS. Advt.— Literary and Philosophical Society Annual Meeting. I The annual meeting of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society was held in the Lecture Hall, Museum-street, on Monday evening, the retiring President, Alderman Bennett, in the chair.— Mr. Robert Dobson' the hon. secretary, read the 37th annual report. There was, he said, a slight increase in the number of the members —l5l as contrasted with 147. The session opened on the 15th October last when Mr. J. T. Foard read an able paper on "The proper place of Shakespeare in Literature." He had in his possession a letter from Mrs. Foard in which she told him that her husband was engaged in correct- ing, the proofs of his paper to be printed in the lecords of the society the' whole of Wednesday morning, the 23rd January, the day of his fatal seizure; in fact .they fell on the floor beside him when he became unconscious never to speak again. The session had been a successful one.—Mr. William Silcock (hon. . treasurer) made a brief sintement as to the financial position of the society, from which it appeared that there was a small balance in hand. • The retiring officers were heartily thanked for their : services during the year.—Mr. Grosvenor moved that ' Mr. A. J. Jolley be the president for the ensuing I year, Alderman Bennett vice-president, Mr. W. Silcock hon. treasurers Mr. Dobson hon. secretary, and the Rev. C. Harvey Cook, Mr. F. G. Ruddock, and Mr. E. J. Hall, members of the Council.—Mr. Sherburn seconded, and the proposition was . unanimously agreed to. PREMIER IN NAME, Premier in quality. Premier Cycles from sevem guineas.—Sole agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. Presentation to Mr. James Dunbabin. An interesting presentation was made the other j evening at Messrs. J. and W. Dutton's premises in ; Sankey-street, to Mr. James Dunbabin the highly esteemed manager of the firm, who is leaving l Warrington to take up his residence at Altrincham. Mr. Boyle (buyer for the fancy department) presided, and spoke in sympathetic terms of Mr. Dunbabin and his long connection with the firm. They felt that in Mr. Dunbabin they had had a friend who was always willing to give them good advice and do all in his power to help them on the way of success in the business world.—Mr. Lewsey (buyer for the furniture department) said he felt bound to say a few words in I praise of the fine example that Mr. Dunbabin had set ' before them. —Mr. Wilde (cashier) said he had learned to admire and respect Mr. Dun- babin. Personally, he would miss his advice I help and encouragement. At the same time I he wished Mr., Mrs., and Miss Dunbabin every success and prosperity in their future business and private life. (Applause). —Miss Dykes (head dressmaker)pre- Bente(' Mr. Dunbabin with four beautiful solid silver vases, subscribed for by the employes only of the firm. —Mr. Dunbabin tendered his heartfelt thanks for the gifts and fol. the high compliments paid to him by the different speaker's. He referred with pleasure to the , good feeling and friendship that existed between the ' staff, and hoped that the same would continue.—After votes of thanks had been passed, the whole company sang " For he's a jolley good fellow," and gave three hearty cheers for Mr. Dunbabin. " HEtta.ro3 KITCHEN RANGES & Peveril " Fire Grates are unequalled. Inspection invited. Large stock of Wood Chimney Pieces, etc.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt. Early Warrington Books. An interesting paper on " Early Warrington Printed Books " was read by Mr. C. Madeley (curator and librarian) at the meeting of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society, on Monday. The printer whose work was under. review was William Eyres, who came of a printing family and was born in 1732. His father John Eyres, printed in 1734, a broadside copy of the old Warrington charters, which was exhibited as the earliest known product of the Warring- ton press. William Eyres, with his brother, published in 1750 " Eyze's Weekly Journal," or "Warring- ton Advertiser," one of the earliest Lancashire newspapers, which, however, only lived for a few months, The lecturer exhibitd the works issued by Eyres for the tutors and others connected with the Academy, many of them being works of great popularity in their day and some of epoch making importance. Priestly's "History of Electricity " (1707), although the earliest general account of the infant science, might yet be read with approbation. Enfield's " Speaker ' (1774) was for fifty years the standard recitation-book in English schools and formed the litery taste of more than one generation. The climax of Eyres' achievement was reached in Watson's "History of the Earl of Warren and Surrey " (2 vols. 4to. 1782) a privately printed work, evidently produced without regard to expense, and authoritatively spoken of as " one of the most remarkable genealogical works produced in England in the 18th century." Alderman Bennett, in support- ing a vote of thanks said that no Warringtonian need feel ashamed of holding high th 3 honour of his town in face of the books before the audience that evening. The old name of Warrington " The Athens of England," was no misnomer, and many fanciful titles which had been given to many places had been applied with less reason ; certainly Warrington had a past of which any city or town in the country might be proud (Applause). The resolution was put and heartily agreed to, and Mr. Madely briefly returned thanks.

div.head: QUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: QUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
The New Theology. The Rev. John Yonge on the Transcendence
of God.

Preaching at Wycliffe Church on Sunday evening, the Rev. John Yonge took for his subject "The Scriptural doctrine of the transcendence of God." He said there could he no doubt whatever that the doctrine of the immanence of God in man was distinctly and definitely taught in the Bible, but it was easily evident to anyone who carefully studied the Bible that there was another doctrine concerning God and His relation to man which was taught even far more distinctly, far more emphati- cally, and far more repeatedly. That doctrine was the infinite and universal transcendence of God over humanity. It would be easy to occupy the whole time for the sermon that night by the mere quotation of the passages, from cover to cover of the Bible, which declared the infinite and eternal supremacy and superiority of God over all creation and all creatures. That was even the most positive, dog- matic, and absolute of all the Bible doctrines concerning Him. It had been pointed out by many who had lately commented upon the New Theology, that in making the foundation of it the doctrine of the immanence of God in men, its advocates had obscured and hidden out of sight the far more supreme truth of the Divine trans- cendence over men. When for instance, they were told that God and man were so closely united as to be essentially one in nature, so that God was man and that• man was God, and that all men were "parts of God," , were they not exposed totheperilous hallucination that God was lower than they had thought Him to be and that they, despite their imperfection and even sinful- ness, were vastly greater and higher than they had imagined ? They were in danger of losing the needed sense of the Divine greatness, holiness and majesty, under the fascination of the idea that God dwelt in their , very nature, and also in the added glamour of the representation that His presence in the secrets of their being was the very foundation and supreme truth of their faith. The 'divinity of man" had a very fine sound in it ; it was very captivating: it ministered to the eongenial desire for a lofty estimate of human nature. But, to say the least of it, it was exceedingly misleading. It tended very greatly to create serious confusion of thought, and to the ignoring and obliter. tion of the boundless and eternal distinction between the Infinite Creator and the finite creature. They needed to be on their most vigilant guard against any teaching which tended to destroy or lesson their sense of the Infinite and eternal difference existing between the Perfect and Holy God, and imperfect and sinful men. God was the Infinite Creittor, and they were the finite creatures of His hands, absolutely dependent upon Him for ever breath they drew. God was the absolutely Pure arid Perfect, and they were the imperfect and the impure, by reason not only of the imperfection of inherited nature, but also by reason of the added impurities of their own personal thought and life. Whatever of good there might be in them was undoubtedly because of His Spirit which dwell within them—and also because that Divine Spirit did dwell within them in exercise of His transcendent mercy and His supremacy of grace. Now, it would seem to be almost impossible to read the Bible with the most ordinary intelligent attention and fail to be impressed by the manifest and manifold descriptions of the unapproachable transcendence of God. But, as they read that assertion and pourtrayal, they did not gather —what some advocates of the New Theology affirmed to be expressed by the Old Theology—that dod, in His transcendance, was set over against His world, and over against the human race. If indeed, the Old Theology did so pourtray the attitude of God in His excellence and omnipotence of Being, then assuredly the old theology would not be sariptual. In actual reality, however, the doctrine concerning God commonly taught in our day by the Evangelical Churches did not so represent the transcendence of God. They never beard it, he was certain, from that pulpit. l'he supreme and all inclusive truths that "God is Light" and" God is Love "had ever been taught. And search all Scripture through, they would not find any texts which did so fully and completely declare the infinite transcendence of God. In no sense whatever was it a Divine transcendence that was hostile or tyrannical: it was not a transcendence of power over a great weakness and helplessness. But it was transcendence of character and nature, of grace and mercy of love, so consummately sublime that the susceptible human heart reverautly and humbly bowed down to worship and adore, to pray and plead, to invoke pity and pardon, and to hide itself under the shadow of Almighty and transcendent love. To discern the immanence of God in their souls would be to realise the transcendence of God beyond and above all other idea of Him. Salvation lay in that experience. It was the vision of the immanent and the transcendent God revealed as the God willing and mighty to save,that arrested and convicted and converted a man.

div.head: Work of Medical Missions
div.p: The Work of Medical Missions

The excellent work which is being done by the medical missions of the Church Missionary Society was described at a public meeting held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey street, on Monday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) presided and was supported on the platform by a number of the local clergy. There was a fair attendance.—ln the course of a brief address the Mayor expressed regret that greater interest was not taken in the Society by the people of Warrington, as its work was certainly deserving of generous support. The object of the medical missions was to give non- Christian lands the benefit of Western medical science and skill and to provide an opportunity for the 'preaching of the Gospel. The need of such work arose firstly from the great want of the people in most of the non-Christian lands of proper medical attention in, the, hour of sickness, and secondly the great difficulties to be met with in those lands in spread- ing Christianity was partly overcome by means of such agencies as the medical mission which touched the hearts of the people and made them willing to listen. There were forty-eight medical stations in the Church Missionary fields—ten in Africa, five in Palestine, four in Persa, two in Turkish Arabia, 15 in India, ten in China, one in Japan and one in North-West Canada. There were 77 doctors and 52 nurses engaged in the work and last year over 22,000 in-patients and 930,000 out-patients received help. There was a need of £30,000 to pay the expenses of this work during the coming year and he hoped Warrington people would zontribute liberally. (Applause.) Dr. E. J. Baxter, then gave a most interesting account of his thirty years' experiences as a medical missionary in Africa, showing the wonderful good accomplished by the Society. He made a very strong appeal to the andience to help for- ward the work.—The Rev. and Hon. C. F. Cross, Vicar of Stretton, briefly sketched the history of the Society, and pointed out that as their faith was not merely a monument to a glorious past, but a living thing, it behoved them to endeavour to spread Christianity in heathen lands.--The Rev. W. R. Cole, district secre- tary, also addressed the meeting, and a collection was taken in aid of the funds of the Society. A choir and small orchestra, under the conductorship of Mr. E. Wilkes, led the singing of the hymns and rendered the anthem "At even ere the sun was set."

SOMEBODY'S MOTHER

The woman was old, and ragged, and gveY, And bent with the chill of the winter's day. The street was wet, with a recent snow, And the woman's feet were aged and slow. She stood at the crossing, and waited long, Alone, uncared for, amid the throng Of human beings, who passed her by, Nor heeded the glance of her anxious eye. Down the street, with laughter and shout, Glad in the freedom of school let out, Came the boys like a flock of sheep, Hailing the snow, laid white and deep. Past the woman, so old and grey, Hastened the children on their way, Nor offered a helping hand to her, So meek, so timid, afraid to stir, Lest the carriage wheels ot horses' feet Should run her down in the slippery street. At last &came one of the merry troop, The gayest laddie of all the group. He paused beside her, and whispered low, "I'll help you across, if you wish to go." Her aged hand on his strong young arm She placed, and so, without hurt or harm, He guided her trembling feet along:. Proud that his own were firm and strong. Then back again to his friends he went, His young heart happy and content. "She's somebody's mother, boys, you, know, For all she's old, and poor, and slow; And I hope some fellow will lend a hand To help my mother, you understand, If ever so poor, and old, And grey, When her own dear boy is far away." And somebody's mother bowed low .her bend In her home that night, and the prayer she said Was, " Gad be kind to the noble boy. Who is somebody's son, and pride, and joy!" From your loving Nephew, EDWARD GA:RDNER.

div.head: MY DEAR NIECES AND NEPHEWS,-
div.p: MY DEAR NIECES AND NEPHEWS,-

Now' that you've read all the essays what do you think of the Prizes? Wasn't I fair in my decision? I think three of my relations will side with me. Well, congratulations to the winners, and the best of good wishes to the losers. As the 'boy said, "You never know your luck." There's bound to be a turn in the tide, my friends; it's the way of the world, even with grown-ups. Hope is a great lesson to learn; but, after all, it's worth learning. Well, now about the Picture Postcard Competition. We are told that it never rains but it pours. Quite so; only, to tell the truth, it was a very weak sort of pour. I anticipated double the number of cards that I received. I shall not tell you how many I got, but it was something under ten thousand. Probably it is a bit difficult to find many post- cards with a funny verse or joke attached, so I have had to judge the cards sent in from an artistic standpoint. The best one received is a delightful oilette of the Corporation Quay at Arundel, and was sent in by Doris Bond, to whom lam giving the first prize. The verse on the card is entitled, "Susan's Perplexity," and is printed below in the column. The next prize goes to M. Wadsworth, for a card of a genial old chap, sitting smoking in a chair, and his grandson, who is ready for bed, is striking a match on his grandfather's head. The head part on the card is composed of sandpaper. The verse attached to the card is
"He vexed grandpa, when saying good-night, By using his pate to strike a light."
This concludes the weekly chat of
UNCLE NED.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am pleased you have accepted me as a member of the C.C. League. I am sending you a piece of poetry, called, "A Stitch in Time," which I hope you will think good enough to print. With love, From your affectionate Nephew, HAROLD HALL.
A STITCH IN TIME

When her frock displays a hole, Grave as any beadle, Katie shakes her curly poll, Promptly threads her needle. In and out it flicks and flies, ' Soon the task is ended; . Scanning well the darn, she cries, "There, sir, you pre mended ! " Katie knows the olden rhyme— Oh 1 she might. be So she takes a stitch in time, Don't you, Madam Katie?

Here's a timely hint, and sound, Little folks may borrow— When a trifling fault is found, Never say, "To-morrow!" Faults Unchecked, like tiny holes, Rapidly extending, Leave the vesture of our souls Tattered past all mend:ng. Act upon the olden rhyme. Packed with wisdom weiplity; Take the saving stitch in time, Just like Madam Katie.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l see by the paper that yon have accepted me and Dolly as your Nephew and Niece. I am sending you a piece of poetry, which I hope to see in-print. It is called,. "The New Baby." With love from Dolly and myself, I remain, your loving Nephew, HARRY TWEEDALE.

THE NEW BABY. She has my crib, she has my name . (They called me "Baby" 'fore she cPice), And now they just say "Son' " I'll have to grow up pretty quick, Because she has my mother, too. And I don't know what I shall do! . I want her just the same at night, To hold my hand and hug me tight, And sing to me, and let me creep Into her lap, and go to sleep. "My nose is broken," but I know It's not my nose that hurts me so Why, I can feel the 'xacly part; It aches and aches all round my heart.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am sending you the following piece of poetry, which I should like to see in print in the next week's issue of the "Children's Corner League" iit the local paper. The piece of poetry is entitled, "Don't Give up the Ship." Your Nephew, FRED HAWORTH. DON'T GIVE UP THE SHIP. You're on the sea of life, boys, Your ship is stanch and strong; you're sailing smoothly now, boys, But storms will come ere king. Then boldly furl your sails, boys, And let the tempest "rip," Stand bravely by the helm, boys, And ".Don't give up the ship."
As already announced, the Ist prize winner of the Christmas Day Competition was L. G. F. Will L. G. F. please forward me the address where I am to dispatch the prize to?

div.head: SUSAN'S PERPLEXITY,
div.p: SUSAN'S PERPLEXITY,

I wonder what the spider spied, And just what sighs the cider sighed, And what is in the willow's will, And has the pillow got a pill; I wonder what the seaweeds see, And if a bullock has a key. I wonder all day long, oh dear, At many other things as queer.
DORIS BOND.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am sending you a short story, ,zhich I hope to see in print, as I think it is a very nice one.
A FIRESIDE FABLE

Some young ducks were swimming on a pond, whilst a nightingale poured forth hi S song. , For a time they listened, and then they shook their heads. "How much better we should under- stand him," said one, "if he would. simply say, 'Quack, quack 1'" With this the rest agreed. From your loving Niece, GWENDOLINE KIVELL.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am writing to tell you I want to join your society, or, rather, "Corner." lam only twelve on March 12th. Here is a story, which I hope you will find room for. A little girl, who, though small, loved to be kind to other people. One day she went to a friend, who was very ill. To extenditer kind- ness she bought some flowers. When she came into the room she exclaimed, "Here, Lucy, I have brought these, to show that I am trying to be kind." " Ahl" said Lucy, "and you have begun well." Hoping to be a Nephew. I remain, sincerely yours, HAROLD JONES.
Dear Uncle Ned,—l hope you have not for- gotten that I am one of your nieces. Will you please send me a bottle of Mason's Extract of Herbs I will send you some poetry later on. Your loving Niece,
MAY BRIGGS.

R 3 5 15 Leeds 2 2 10 Thelwall l3 4 3 6 *Huddersfield Hunslet 2 2 10 *Batley 1 1 5 Orford Barracks Bradfosd *Broughton R 2 3 13 Hull *St. Helens *Oldham *Wakefield Trinity 4 9 35 Brs.mley 0 2 6 SECOND DIVISION. *Leigh 22 14 4 4 41 *Keighley 2O 9 2 9 38 2 Swinton 3 2 12 Liverpool City 2 2 10 Halton A.F.C. 1 2 8 *Warrington ... 0 1 3 : Castner Kellner Reserve Penketh Athletic lB 9 3 6 52 30 ' Oughtrington Park Reserve 18 8 3 7 50 15 Latchford Crescent 22 10 9 3 40 38 Warrington St. Paul's St. Barnabas Reserve lB 8 7 3 27 29 Warrington were accompanied to Swinton by a large Orford A.F.C. 22 610 6 30 44 number of followers on Saturday. It was generally Christ Church Reserve expected that the visitors would win, and in fact it was Warrington St. Elphin's essential for them to do so in order to secure one of Sankey St. Mary's l6 312 1 15 34 the coveted top four place's in the League. With the Walker's Blewery exception of Jenkins and Boardman, Warrington were I Ryland! Reserve) l7 213 2 11 45 at full strength,and Swinton wereolso fully represented. I Daresbury withdrawn. Record expunged. Unfortunately the weather turned out wet and the IMatches for March 16th. ground was little better than a swamp at 3.30 when the Thelwall v. Oughtrington Park; referee, J. Lloyd. match started. Teams : Swinton.—Fielding, back; Griffin, Wallwork, Valen- • St. Barnabas• v. Warrington Albions ; refetee, C. \ tine and Jones, three-quarter backs ; Booth and Cowell, Taylor. Palatine v. Castner Kellner ; referee, J. Mather. half backs ; Sinister (captain), Barnett, Pomfret, Hob- Christ Church Reserve v. Halton : referee, S. G. Platt son, Davies, and Lloyd, forwards. Latchford Crescent v. Warrington St. Elphin's ; Warrington.—Tilley, back ; Fish, Isherwood, Dicken- referee, L. Jones. son, and Brooks, three-quarter backs; Lees and Hecken-' Walkers' v. St. Barnabas' Reserve ; referee, G. Smith. hall, half backs; Thomas, Preston, Heath, Naylor, Oughtrington Park v. Penketh ; referee, C. T. Cox. Shugars, and Harmer, forwards. Sankey St. Mary's v. Christ Church Reserve; referee, Referee, Mr. T. H. Marshall (Bradford). Touch J. „- judges, Messrs T. Smith (Rochdale) and W. J. Britton •Parry. (Leigh). Warrington started off with strong forward play and Thomas charged a return by Wallwork, but the ball went dead. Swinton put on pressure after this, and Davies missed a penalty kick in front of tke posts. The ground seemed to upset the Warrington men, and they rarely passed with precision. Still they more than held the home lot, and after about a cluarter of an hour's fruitless play the first score came. Lees got cleverly round the scrum in the Swinton quarter, and throwing wide to Dickenson the latter ran across and served Fish, who raced over at the corner. Preston made a good attempt at goal. Almost immediately on resum- ing, Warrington's joy was turned to disappointment. Lees fumbled a catch near the line, and then kicked the ball against Tilley with the result that Griffin had a walk-over near the posts. Wallwork missed an easy goal-shot and the team were on level terms. Swinton attacked strongly after this, but their methods were not very scientific, and Warrington easily held them at bay. Half-time: One try each. On resuming, Warrington had the advantage of the slope and a slight breeze, and were expected to show to more advantage. Disaster early befel them, however. Within three minutes of the start Isherwood made a fly-kick at the ball in mid-fieldana missed with the result that the Swinton forwards rushed the ball past Tilley and over the line under the posts. Wallwork added the goal. This was a disaster for Warrington' and one that. might have been avoided. For the next few minutes they attacked strongly. Fish ran down touch and passed inside near the line, the forwards missing a grand chance. Several cross-kicks were tried, but Fielding was very safe and eventually the home forwards by smart footwork took the ball to the other end where Tilley saved pluckily. Warrington were kept almost entirely on the defensive to the close, the Swinton men seeming to keep their feet much better in the mud than Warrington. Brooks once got clear away in his own quarter. but Wallwork overhauled-him at centre. Fish was off part of the time with an injury to his wrist. Final :—Swinton, one goal two tries (8 points) ; Warrington, one try (3 points).

div.head: MATCHES ON MONDAY.
div.p: MATCHES ON MONDAY.
Halifax V. Warrington.

This thrice-postponed match took place at Halifax on Monday evening in beautiful weather, before 10,000 spectators. Both teams were well represented, Warring- ton replacing Fish and Harmer with Jordan and Board- man. Teams :-- _ _

Halifax: Little, back; W. J. Williams, Ward, Joe Riley, and Eccles, three-quarter backs; Hilton and Grey, half backs; Bartle, Brearley, Littlewood, Lang- horn, Robinson, and FL Morley, forwards. Warrington: Berry, back ; Jordan, Isherwood, Dickenson, and Brooks, three-quarter backs; Lees and Hockenhall, half backs; Thomas Preston, Heath, Naylor, Shugars and Boardman, forwards. -Referee, Mr. Kennedy, Broughton. 'Pouch judges, Messrs. Renton, Hunslet, and Sewell, Leeds. Little started the game, and for a time Halifax attacked strongly, first Joe Riley and then Williams being tickled when dangerous. Isherwood transferred play to centre, but Hilton at length dodged cleverly over between the uprights, and added the goal points. The Warrington forwards were then seen to advantage, and the home line was reached. Little cleared his lines finely, and Joe Riley with a run and kick sent the ball rolling into touch beyond the half way line. Grey received the ball from Hilton, and running to within a few yards of the line, he re-passed to Hilton who easily scored. The goal kick by Hilton was again successful Dickenson soon afterwards was injured, and retired, Thomas coming out of the pack into the threequarter line. Halifax again got dangerous, and Grey, taking a pass from Hilton. scored in an easy position. Hilton kicked agl from the place. Berry, the Warrington full back, soon afterwards gained half the length of the field, and finished up a good effort by sending into touch in the home" 25." Halifax returned to the attack and a dribble by the forwards, in which H. Morley took a conspicuous part, ended in Lan ghorn crossing the line, and Hilton added another goal to the Halifax score. Half-time—Halifax 4 goals, 4 tries (20 points), 'Warrington nil. Halifax were quickly dangerous after the interval,and Williams was pushed into touch near the line by Thomas. Halifax forced a minor, and then lost the services of Hilton. Berry, the Warrington full back, also retired with an injury to his leg, and the visitors were two men short for the remainder of the game. Eccles scored for Halifax, and Little kicked a goal. Hockenhall soon afterwards broke away finely, but Little charged the ball, and sent it rolling into touch close to the visitors' line. Joe Riley from the next scrummage dashed over, and Little from a very difficult place kicked a tine goal. W. J. Williams next completed a good passing move- ment, and scored far out, but this time Little failed at goal. Brearley soon afterwards made a mark just insiee the Warrington half, and Little kicked a fine goal. Halifax continued to hold the upper hand, but nothing further was scored. lteiudt :—Halifax 7 goals tties (35 points), Warrington nil,

div.head: RUNCORN v. YORK.
div.p: RUNCORN v. YORK.

This postponed match was plaed at Runcorn on ! Monday. Each team had several changes. ?Hamer started, and a mistake by Jolley resulted in York atiack- ing strongly near the home line. Harrison relieved, after which Runcorn gained further ground. Moran passed to Hesketb, who scored, butJolley failed at goal. Immediately afterwards Plimmer placed a fine penalty goal for York. Walker, Flanagan, and Moran then added a try each in quick succession, Jolley being successful with one of the goal kicks. Before the interval J. Williams scored a try for Runcorn, which Jolley converted, whilst Hughes scored for York after a fine effort, Plimmer failing at goal. Hal f-time Runcorn, two goals, five tries (19 points) ; York, one goal, one try (5 points). In the second portion York were completely out- classed. Benny and Daniels did good work behind the pack, but were unable to check the home halves, who initiated some fine passing movements. Flanagan (2) and Moran scored tries, which neither Richardson nor :Tolley could convert. Near the close of the game Ilesketh scored again, whilst MacDonald addcd two more tries. Jolley placed goals from the last three tries. The result practically assures Runcorn of a place among the first four clubs. Result—Runcorn, five goals and 11 tries (43 points) ; York, one goal and one try (five points).
• WAKEFIELD TRINITY v. OLDHAM. Played at Wakefield, the visitors winning by three goals:2 tries (12 points) to nil.

div.head: LANCASNIRE COMBINATION.
div.p: LANCASNIRE COMBINATION.
WARRINGTON "A" v. PEMBERTON.

This match was played at Wilderspool on Saturday before a large attendance. Warrington early became aggressive, but reckless passing spoiled several good openings, and from one of these failures the right wing of the visitors got cleverly away and raced in for a good try, which wss improved. Warrington forwards followed up a kick by Cartwright and the Pemberton backs hesitating, Jolley took the ball over and scored a try. The goal-kick was a failure. Warrington still pressed hard, and Taylor and Hewitt made bold attempts to cross. Rallying, near the interval, the visitors got dangerous. At half-time Pemberton led by five points to three. In the second half the visitors early increased their advantage when one of the centre threequarters dropped a goal. The Warrington forwards improved in the later stages, and Morley, a new forward, hailing from Irlam, sc9rfia:l an unconverted try. The game was especially exciting in the last few minutes, when Taylor placed a penalty goal for the home men and won the match by the odd point. Final :—Warrington, one goal two tries (eight points) ; Pemberton, two goals one try (seven points). C. T. P. G. T. P. Wigan A 43 Salford A 0 1 3 Wigan Highfield... 1 3 11 Runcorn A. 0 1 3

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

BAND OF HOPE CONCERT.—Under the auspices of the I Hill Cliffe and Stockton Heath United Band of Hope an entertainment was given in the Providenct, school- room, on Monday evening, at which the programme was provided entirely by the younger members. Miss Ada, Mountield presided over the first part of the programme. This young lady, in a neat little speech, spoke of the necessity of being Band of Hive members and carried out her duties in an admirable manner. Miss Emma Hamblett delivered her maiden speech in capital style and was heartily applauded. The second part was in the , hands of the sterner sex. Master Ernest Musson I acquitted himself very creditably as chairman and Master Harry Earle delivered an able address. During the evening songs were gives by Dolly Caird (encored), Bessie Pearce, Elsie Whitfield (encored), Edith Hughes, Carry Cain, Elsie and M. MOuntield, It. Lonsdale, and E. Hamblett, all of which were much enjoyed; recita- tions by E. Grounds, M. Speaksrnan, M. Cain, M. Earle, W. Smith, T. Richmond, G. t litre, A. Cliffe, E. Dearne and M. Kirkland. Master T. Pearce contributed an organ solo, and the following dialogues were well given : "The coming woman" by seven girls," Band of Hope brigade" by six boys, "The sewing class " by eight girls," Only port wine " by senior girls, and " Fishirrg " by A. Whitfield and B. Isherwood. The action song " We are temperance children" was much enjoyed as were also the gramophone selections giuen by Mr. T. Richmond. On the motion of Mr. A. Whitfield (secre- tary), a vote of thanks was accorded to all who had taken part in the molting. Messrs. A. Whitfield and Thomas Pearce acted as accompanists.

div.head: CYCLE WITH ONE WHEEL.
div.p: CYCLE WITH ONE WHEEL.
Mr. Henry To!cher, of Pretoria, has invented a cycle with only one wheel. He claims that the machine will cover between thirty and forty miles an hour on level ground.

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.

The Guardians and Out-Relief. Sir,—As there seems to be a general impression in the town that the Guardians of the Poor do not give out-relief, I feel it is only fair to my fellow workers to explain that we give £215 every fortnight in out- relief. Of course one has no right to be lax in the dis- tribution of public funds, and each case is most care- fully considered and investigated. This takes one hour every fortnignt, besides the five hours of close work which we give every half-year to the revision of the whole.—Yours, Scc., CONSTANCE H. BROADBENT. " The Voice of Labour." Sir,—You are to be congratulated upon your new venture in deciding to set apart a portion of the " Examiner " for the consideration and discussion of Labour and Social questions. I have often thought that the managers of the local papers were lacking in enterprise by neglecting to take advantage of the labour " boom " which can be said to date from the last General Election. Since that Election, which resulted in the return of so many Labour Members to the House of Commons, there has been a growing demand for information regarding the principles and work of the Labour and Socialist parties. This interest in labour and social questions is not confined entirely to what are called the working classes, but a (Treater spirit of inquiry is being shown by the middle and upper classes, which can be proved by the large number of articles on Labour ques- tions which are now appearing in our leading journals. I trust that the "Voice of Labour" will not be the voice of the manual workers only. "Labour," when nued by us who are Socialists, means all those who are con- tributing, either by hand or brain, to the wealth of the nations. Those of us who follow the local press closely, must agree that the "Examiner" takes the lead in their reports of trades-unionism and labour meetings, and in their comments and criticisms of the Labour movement. I trust, therefore, that the workers of Warrington will support you in this experiment, and that in the near future its success will be so proaonnced that more space will be required for the consideration of those ques- ti,ins which so vitally affect their interests.—Sincerely yours,

FRED STOTT. Mr. McKenna's Education Bill. Sir,—Will you permit me to trouble you with a few lines of criticism on the provisions of this Bill. The Bill proposes to lay a charge upon the schools of £6 13s. per cent. on all salaries paid to the teachers in denominational schools or one fifteenth of the whole amount of such salaries, this proportion being supposed to represent the proportion of time given by the teachers to religious instruction. I would point out that this proposal is really an attempt to put a fine on denominational schools simply because they are denominationo.l, and so further accen- tuate the unfair and unequal treatment to which the denominational schools are already subjected. Hitherto schools have only been mulcted for ineffi- ciency, the standard of efficiency having reference to the secular instruction only. Now it is proposed to depart from this rule as regards the denominational schools, so that though the work of secular instruction may bedone as efficiently in these schools as in other schools, it shall nevertheless be paid for only on a lower scale of remuneration. The injustice of this is obvious. It is well known that in the past the denominational schools have held their own in competition with all other schools as regards efficiency in secular subjects, the government itself being the judge, and applying their own tests at the periodical examinations. Worst of all the Government proposal embodies the false and vicious principle that giving its proper place to religious instruction in the gensral education of the child is a drawback to the secular instruction, whereas it may very easily be contended from the very highest examples that the reverse is the case; and it is this conviction that leads Churchmen to accept any sacrifices rather than send their children to schools from which • religious teaching is excluded. And then even from a secular point of view there is much that is of value in the giving of relinious instruc- tion which nevertheless the Government Bill ignores. The memory at least is as much exercised by this teach- ing as by any other teaching; even the reading lesson is still a reading lesson though it be given from the Bible. And the history of the Jek\ ish people is quite as much history as the history of the English people. Even moral duty, which the Government seems desirous of turning into a secular subject, is as much moral duty when taught on the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ as on the authority of some author selected by a Local Education Authority. These considerations render Mr. McKenna's attempt th estimate by a fraction the proportion that religious instruction bears to secular instruction in a denomina- tional school as simply ridiculous. It will be gathered from this that this attempt to penalize the teaching of the Church of England, is in my opinion at once unjust, intolerant, absurd and even Anti-Christian.--I am, &c.,
E. C. E. CARLETON.

The Government and Unemployment. Sir.—l have no particular desire to criticise adversely the present Government because I willingly recognise that in their short administrative career they have placed, with the valuable aid of a certain amount of gentle persuasion from the Labour Party, two or three beneficial and constructive measures of legislation on the Statute Book affecting the material interests of = millions of my fellow workers. But it is evident that no serious intention exists amongst the select few that rule the destinies of our country to deal with the unemployment question. To me this is a matter ef great regret. I feel confident if our wealthy legislators could only realise what horrors unemployment brings in its trail not only to the individual affected but the community to-day and the generation to-morrow, we would have less political window dressinc,, and a more serious attempt to deal With a question that I venture to say is closely con- nected with our national physique and bulwark of defence. The other week when Mr. Will Thorne moved his unemployed amendment to the address, out of a House of 670 members, 47 stalwarts voted in favour of the amendment. There are 398 Liberals in the Commons, and there were just 10 found to posses sufil- ,cient courage to disobey the Party Whip, and join with the Independent Labour group to bring pressure on the Government to deal with this vital matter. Ffind that the following 18 Liberals: Sydney Buxton, R. K. Canston, Charles Fenwick, Herbert Gladstone, R. B. Haldane, C. E. H, Hobhouse, Sir W. H. Holland, H. E. Kearley, Sir Joseph F. Leese, J. IL Lewis J. Lloyd Morgan, Captain Norton, J. H. Roberts, John Sinclair, Sir Alfred Thomas, a A. Thomas, T. C. T. Warner and Eugene Mason opposed Mr. Keir Hardie's Unem- ployed Amendment to the Address in 1893 when the Liberals were in power, supported Mr. Keit. Hardie's Unemployed Amendment in 1903 when the Liberals were in opposition and now when the Liberals are in Rowe: again they record their votes against Mr. Will 7iorne's unemployed amendment. This is surely a further•proof that party exigencies count for more than pririciple. I say this question deserves immediate attention. Sir Edward Verney has given us a terse and axiomatic definition of the unemployed. There are rifted few economic facts which have been presented Inn swifter and more precise terms than the following whilichs article on "The iniquities of the Poor Law" (Octobe aPpears of the 145). in the "Contemporary Review" 19415). "The The unemployed exist for the benefit the e rich; when not wanted they are maint,ained at expense of the ratepayers. work Yours, et&,, theY are brought out to keep wages down."—
GAS WORKER.

div.head: PROSPEROUS ASSURANCE COMPANY.
div.p: A PROSPEROUS ASSURANCE COMPANY.

The remarkable prosperity of the Prudential Assur- ance Company Ltd. is once more brought to the notice of the public by the issuing of the annual balance sheet which appears in our advertising columns. This great concern transacts the largest amount of ordinary life assurance business of any British company and with the addi,tion to the annual bonus now delared—the bonus is now 32s.per cent.per annum—seems likely to far eclipse its own previous records. During 1906 it issued no fewer than 79,912 policies assuring £7,529,031, producing a new annual income of £424,145 and bringing the premium income for the year to £4,290,971, an increase of £167,653 over 1905. During the year 7,656 claims and 8,686 maturing endowments absorbed £1,947,444. The total assets increased by £4,422,632, and now amount to over sixty-three and three-quarter millions. The Prudential is one of the most economical in both the industrial and the ordinary branches. Its expenses in the ordinary department are but 8.7 per cent of the annual premiums against an average of the remaining British offices of 14 per cent. But despite these low expenses the Prudential progress has in 1906 been extremely rapid. There was an increased premium income of over £l,OOO a day in the tndustrial business only, which is double the increase in 1905. The unfortunate wreck of the " Berlin "is fresh in the public mind. The number of fatalities amongst the crew was 46, some of the lost were foreigners, yet, notwithstanding this fact, 20 were assured with the Prudential. Seven of the passengers were also assured. These 27 persors among them held 39 policies, 27 in the Industrial Branch and 12 in the Ordinary Branch, and the total sums assured exceeded £2,440. Mr. J. T. Rowlands, Sankey-street, is the energetic superintendent of the Warrington district.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.
[By " Ovalist."]
It will take a lot of Cup-tie tonic to revive the Warrington supporters after the experiences of last weekend: All hope of the local team appearing. in

the first four has 'r-anished as the result of successive defeats by Swinton and Halifax. At the critical moment Warrington failed and failed badly. They now stand in the comparatively lowly position of eighth, and as the compositioA of the first four has to be decided after April 2nd in order that the deciding ties may played off there is not much chance of them retrieving their position even though there are five League matches to be played before that date is passed. Warrington should pass Hunslet, Leeds and Keighley in the race but that would only bring them to .the fifth pla3e and they will not reach that if defeat is sustained at Runcorn and Huddersfield. Hope of the League championship may be, I think, abandoned for this season and the efforts of the • Club concentrated on the Cup-ties.

Warrington's form at present is very disappointing, and in fact has been so ever since the end of January. The postponements due to frost seemed to throw the side out of gear completely, and there has been none of the old-time brilliance since. The display at Swinton on Saturday was lamentable. Instead of winning pretty comfort- ably as expected Warrington shaped like a third-rate side and were inferior to the homesters all through. Still they might have won if the defence had been as reliable as usual. Warrington held the lead once, but two tries were afterwards given to their opponents through nothing but bad play. On the attack War- rington were singularly weak and unenterprising and never caused the homesters much anxiety.

Possibly the state of the ground had something to do with Warrington's poor form. It was little better than a mud-heap, and fast open play was almost an impossibility. Warrington rarely do well under these conditions and they certainly failed to adapt them- selves to the occasion like the homesters. Swinton were lighter forward, but they excelled in dribbling and following up. When the ball had to be " played " they invariably got possession no matter how many Warrington men were behind the oval. It was only in the scrums that Warrington's weight was effective and the spotting was so close and the Warrington back play so feeble that heeling out was worth little. A strong, speedy half-back might have altered the aspect of affairs, and Jenkins was much missed. Lees made the only opening. that was made, flockenhall doing very little on the attack. Isherwood and Fish were both below form, and the latter will be no use until he gets his weight down. I might find fault with others but it is little use doing so ; not one was good, and most were bad.

Over Monday's display at Halifax it would be kinder to draw a veil and wait for Good Friday. Only once before have Warrington been beaten by 35 points to nil., and that was at Oldham on November 19th, 1898. Halifax thus tied with the record against Warrington and it is something to be thankful for that they did not break it. There is some excuse for Warrington's collapse. Halifax certainly had all the luck of the game, and in addition Dickenson and Berry were both so injured that they had to retire, the first-named quite early on. Halifax were in-tip-top -form and Hilton. the ex-Leigh half played a marvellous game until he was hurt in the second half. Up to half time he sdbred 4 goals 2 tries. To-day he is the best half back in Yorkshire, and it is not long since Leigh declined to find him a regular place on their team.
Monday was the first occasion on which Warrington had been beaten pointless this season. May it be the last!
